utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. I would like now to explain how we are going to proceed during this hearing. As the registrar announced, today we are hearing the case of the Prosecutor against Stanislav Galic. The charges against Mr. Galic stem from military encirclement of the city of Sarajevo from 1992 to 1994 by Bosnian Serb forces. Mr. Galic and the Prosecution appeal from the judgement rendered on 5 December 2003 by Trial Chamber I, composed of Judge Orie, presiding, and Judges El Mahdi and Nieto-Navia. The Trial Chamber by a majority found Mr. Galic guilty of acts of violence, the primary purpose of which was to spread terror among the civilian population, a violation of the laws or customs of war, as set forth in Article 51 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions of 1949; murder as a crime against humanity through sniping; inhumane acts other than murder as crimes against humanity through sniping; murder as a crime against humanity through shelling; and inhumane acts other than murder as crimes against humanity through shelling. As a consequence of the finding of guilt it entered on Count 1, the Trial Chamber dismissed Counts 4 and 7 concerning attacks on civilians as set forth in Article 51 of Additional Protocol I and Article 13 of Additional Protocol II to the Geneva Conventions of 1949 as a violations of the laws or customs of war. Mr. Galic was sentenced to a single sentence of 20 years' imprisonment. I will now briefly summarise the grounds of appeal of Mr. Galic. Mr. Galic now brings 19 grounds of appeal. In grounds 1 through 3, Mr. Galic alleges infringement of his right to fair trial, including his right to testify at trial; an alleged error in failing to disqualify Judge Orie; and an alleged error in failing to conduct a site visit to Sarajevo. In grounds 4, 11 and 13, Mr. Galic alleges errors in use of evidence. In ground 4, Mr. Galic alleges that the Prosecution failed to disclose exculpatory evidence in a timely manner. In grounds 11 and 13, Mr. Galic alleges the Trial Chamber erred in its approach to the evaluation of evidence. In grounds 5, 7 and 16, Mr. Galic alleges errors in the Trial Chamber's finding in relation to his conviction for the crime of terror. Grounds 6 through 18 allege errors in relation to Mr. Galic's convictions for murder and inhumane acts. In part, he alleges errors concerning the Trial Chamber's legal findings related to the crime of attacks against civilians, cumulative convictions and a determination of his individual criminal responsibility. Mr. Galic also alleges errors in the Trial Chamber's consideration of collateral damage in the definition of terms in the trial judgement and the Trial Chamber's consideration of the alleged campaign of shelling and sniping against the civilian population of Sarajevo. Ground 19 concerns his appeal against the sentence. The Prosecution brings one ground of appeal against the sentence. During the hearing, the Appellant's counsel may argue the grounds of appeal in the order they consider most suitable for their presentation. However, I wish to note and remind the parties that by the Scheduling Order issued by the Appeals Chamber of -- on 14 August 2006, the Appeals Chamber has invited the parties to develop further their submissions on certain issues. The Appeals Chamber has fully considered the submission of the parties in writing and would like to have oral arguments on the issues as mentioned in the Scheduling Order of 14 August 2006. I would now like to recall the criteria applicable to errors of fact and law alleged on appeal. The appeal is not a trial de novo and the appellants must not merely repeat their case from the trial level. Rather, in accordance with Article 25 of the Statute of the Tribunal, the appellants must limit their arguments to alleged errors of law which invalidate the decision or alleged error of fact occasioning a miscarriage of justice. Additionally, it should be recalled that the appellants have an obligation to provide precise references to materials supporting their arguments on appeal. This hearing will proceed according to the Scheduling Order issued on 14 August 2006. Counsel for Mr. Galic will present submissions this morning until 10.55. Following a 30 minutes pause, counsel for the Prosecution will then begin to present a response from 11.25 to 11 -- to 12.25. After the break, between 12.25 and 14.15, counsel for the Prosecution will have time to continue their response from 14.15 to 15. And then we will go accordingly following the Scheduling Order. I will not repeat all the times now. I will remind the parties of the time when we come to the -- to their presentations. Bearing in mind that the hearing of the whole appeal, including the appeal of the Prosecution, shall conclude at 5.20 in the afternoon. It will be most helpful to the Appeals Chamber if the parties could present their submissions in a precise and clear manner. The Judges as usual may interrupt the parties at any time to ask questions or they may ask questions following each party's submissions as they will seem -- would deem it appropriate. Having said this about the manner in which we'll proceed today, I would now like to invite counsel for Mr. Galic to present their arguments in support of his appeal. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, in accordance with the Scheduling Order for this appeals hearing, the Defence will do its best to, within the allotted time, first answer the questions that were put to the Defence, starting from the judgement and the sentence, where sniping incidents and shelling incidents were analysed separately, the Defence will first answer questions 1, 2 and 4 pertaining to the shelling, following which I will answer the second question and provide the analysis of response for questions 3 and 5. I would like to yield the floor to my friend, Piletta-Zanin. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I hesitated for a long time before coming before this Chamber to present the position of General Galic and his Defence team. The reason why I give you these authorities is the following. We know that in this case the -- General Galic was prosecuted for the offences you summed up at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]. Your Honour, we are pressed for time, so I suppose I can proceed. I wanted to say the following. General Galic was prosecuted and convicted for a number of offences but we have to remember one thing. Whilst he was being tried, amongst the three Judges who were sitting at trial, you had a Presiding Judge who had already taken a decision with regard to prima facie evidence when confirming the indictment against General Mladic. When he confirmed the indictment, the Presiding Judge, Mr. Orie, clearly, publicly stated as a judge, that General Galic was also likely to be prosecuted as an accomplice to General Mladic as part of a joint criminal enterprise of genocide. Therefore, we have a situation where a Presiding Judge is sitting at trial for crimes such as murders of a lesser level than that of genocide, genocide that is being presented as the most -- as the crime of crimes. We have a Presiding Judge who is sitting at trial for someone who is prosecuted for murder but has confirmed an indictment with regard to genocide. How can we admit, how can we accept objectively or subjectively that an accused, whoever he is, Galic, or anyone else, can reasonably prepare his defence when he's being faced with a Presiding Judge who has already considered that he might be, there is prima facie evidence that he might be guilty of genocide? I can tell you that all the authorities that could have ruled on this, for example, the International Court for Human Rights in Strasbourg, all of these institutions would state that the said judge would have to be disqualified. That's what I wanted to say as a way of introduction, and that was why principles have to be complied with. This being said, let me now move on to another aspect of this trial. The qualification of the trial, and I'm talking about the crime of terror, that is a new word, a new concept, because the Tribunal has invented a new word at least in French, the crime of terrorisation. And this is the second point I would like to stress, the second violation against my client. We have an accused who was prosecuted for a crime that had been previously prosecuted according to the Rules with an indictment that was confirmed by a Judge of a Tribunal according to Rule 50, and this crime that was pleaded in the indictment is accepted by the Tribunal. Mr. Ierace is here so he's not going to contradict me. This trial means that the actual infliction of terror has to be proven, terror that was inflicted on the population. The trial took place under those circumstances with the idea confirmed that the Tribunal, that the Prosecution has to adduce evidence of the actual infliction, and this evidence was never adduced. At the end of the Prosecution case, the Defence case started, quite logically, and the Defence focused its case on other elements than the so-called crime of terror. Why? Why? Because according to us, the evidence had not been adduced as to the crime of terror, so there was no need for us to stress or to focus on that matter. And at the end of the trial, once the Defence and the Prosecution had finished their job, what we found was that the Judges were not even unanimous in their decision, a very weak majority of two Judges. When you consider what is at stake here, these two Judges requalified the offence, after 18 months, without ever having asked a single question to anyone. What they said, these Judges, was that what was needed was not to prove that terror had been inflicted. What needed to be proven was whether there were acts committed that were likely to provoke terror. Therefore, they founded themselves on the definition of Article 51. Therefore, they prevented the Defence to focus on that issue, and that's clear, very clear. Unfortunately for General Galic, this is a violation of his basic rights. Let me now turn to the concept of civilian population, but I'd like to check how much time I have left. And I keep in mind the questions you raised under point 1 and 2 -- or point 1 of the Scheduling Order you quoted earlier on, the Scheduling Order of the 14th of August, 2006. You asked a pivotal question, I'll come back to that later, but as for these attacks that are considered by the Defence as being admitted wrongly by the Trial Chamber as being unlawful, that is to say including targeting of a civilian population, a deliberate targeting of a civilian population, we are going to proceed as follows. I'm going to examine the five cases of scheduled shelling that were submitted to the Trial Chamber, and I'm also going to consider a number of findings of the Trial Chamber point by point, in order to verify why an attack that has been considered as lawful cannot be considered as such. Is there a problem with the interpretation? Because I'm not listening or is everything going smoothly? Well, then I'll proceed. Mr. President, we perfectly know what civilian objects are, and even if we go by Additional Protocol I, we can use the negative definition usually given by the text, that is to say, that civilian assets are those that are not military objectives. Talking about Additional Protocol I and to assist the Chamber, I would like to say that contrary to what has always been stated, it seems that the agreement of the 22nd of May, 1992, might never have come into force because the ICRC confirmed to me that when they never received that agreement, they've looked it up in their archives and they've never found these four letters of confirmations that would have been in -- necessary but I see that I'm being interrupted again, so I'll give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: I'm so sorry to interrupt again but my friend is now going into evidence that is not in the record. In fact, this was something that was dealt with in, I believe it was the second additional evidence motion which was dismissed, and we would ask that he not give evidence about this matter from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is just a mere detail. You know that the Trial Chamber made their decision based on letters that they went to look for in -- at the library of the Tribunal so you can do exactly the same. You can go to the library of the Tribunal and find these letters, because I myself gave that letter very generously to the library here for this document to be used by anyone. This document is to be found at the library. May I proceed because we are wasting time here. Thank you very much. I'm lost here. I hope that I will be granted additional time because of all these interruptions. What I wanted to say is if you want to state that Additional Protocol I was applicable, the first thing is that when it comes to unlawful attacks you first have to define civilian object as opposed to military objects. If you do not conduct that exercise, and that was absolutely essential, that was a task that had to be fulfilled by the Trial Chamber, then you cannot come to any conclusion. You cannot give any answer to the question you asked under point 2 of your Scheduling Order, that is to say, whether attacks on apparently legitimate objectives can be such that they can imply terror through the application of the principle of proportionality that allegedly was not applied in that case. But I'll come to that later. If that exercise is not being conducted, then nothing can be ruled. I'm going to quote a number of points here by the Trial Chamber or a number of witnesses, Francis Roy Thomas, 30th of May, 2002, and I quote: "[Previous translation continues] ... headquarters or was close to the confrontation line, most of Sarajevo, the Sarajevo that I knew would fall under the category of residential area." [Interpretation] Very well. But then we have to know where their headquarters are, and this is where the problem arose in practical terms. In order to assist the Chamber, I would like to give the following references as far as transcript are concerned. 4733, 6149, 6222, and especially but always by way of an example, 8668, with the testimony of Mole, whom I'm going to quote. "[Previous translation continues] ... sir, that the shelling was indiscriminate. Could you tell us precisely where the HQs of the Brigades, HQs of the battalions, and the HQs of the companies? "Answer: On which side, sir? "Question: In Sarajevo. "Answer: No, sir. I can't." [Interpretation] So, there is it is. This is what the witness stated. He was a high-ranking officer of UNMO and he represented the general opinion. These people did not know where the barracks were, barracks of the main military sites, or even posts such as command posts, so how on earth do you know if there is a shelling allegedly taking place in town, how can they exclude the fact that it might not be a legitimate and lawful shelling? It fell on a neighbourhood, it was obviously civilian for them. But if you look at the facts, they did not know where the legitimate objectives were, and even the general in charge of the operation didn't know. You see Abdel-Razek, 15th of July, 2000, transcript 11616 and following. He confesses that he did not -- it was not aware of such locations. Fraser, 11210, 11220 and 223. Now, five shelling incidents, scheduled incidents, they mainly concern three areas, three geographical areas out of ten Sarajevo neighbourhoods, and they cover only 15 days in all. For the first two scheduled shelling incidents, January 1994, 22nd of January, 1994, and 5th of February, 1994. With regard to incident 3, 4 and 5, and 42 days, as I said earlier, for the first two scheduled shelling incidents, 1st of June, 1993, and 12th of July, 1993. These are incidents 1 and 2. Out of an overall figure of 2 -- 720 days, two years, in other words, by way of example we only have a period of less than two months. This is very decisive. All the more so because there is not one single incident of this whole campaign, alleged campaign, from the time of -- when General Galic takes function in September 1992 to September 1994. So there you have only three shelling incidents out of 15 days. And this is at a time when the military situation was very tense, when the Serbs were asking for peace agreements, when the parties were resolutely against it, some wanted NATO to intervene, military, by an air -- by air strikes as history has shown us. In the three scheduled shelling incidents on Dobrinja, on the south area of the town, two are obviously cases that cannot be regarded as attacks on civilians. The first one, the one that was erroneously called the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This happened --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]. Well, if the origin of the shelling can be proved, they are going to try and focus on the entry or the exit of the tunnel. In this respect, it appeared recently, and the Defence will endeavour to adduce the evidence as quickly as it can, it appeared recently that letters coming from the Supreme Command of Sarajevo at the time, from the Presidency, establish that the Muslim forces had created a fake entrance to that tunnel, Dobrinja-Butmir, in the middle of an area with a civilian population, some 1250 metres from the real entrance, which is exactly where the alleged incident of the queue for the water took place. I wanted to attract your attention to this because this is not the system of the human shield where civilians are put in order to hide the objectives. This is an other system which will be proved through letters that we are going to adduce where fake and decoys are used in order to attract shooting or shelling on the civilian population forecasting the consequences. In this respect, and going back to the issue of Dobrinja, I wanted to quote a passage to be found in a report [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] ... to Congress on the conduct of the Persian Gulf War [Interpretation] quoted in Bouvier Sassoli, page 1026. This is such a well known piece of work that I don't need to give the references. I quote: [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] "... lateral civilian casualties. A substantial responsibility for protection of the civilian population rests with the party controlling the civilian population." [Interpretation] Page 1026 and further, equally interesting: [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] "... must exercise reasonable precautions to separate the civilian population and civilian objects from military objectives and avoid placing military objectives in the midst of civilian population." [Interpretation] I remind you that in the said case it was the shelling of a bunker where civilians had sought shelter, and this report I quote never concluded that there was any criminal responsibility of any military leaders in this shelling incident that caused several casualties among civilian population, and it is a very well known case. And this is precisely, precisely what is happening in the two shelling incidents in Dobrinja which I'm now quoting, the one of June and the one of July 1993. Indeed. How can you admit supposing that the source of file was Serbian, how can you admit that it would be acceptable that in time of war, an authority that is supposed to protect its own civilian population would authorise civilians to come and organise a football game on basically the front line? This is a distance counted in metres, not in kilometres, and there was the front line, next door to it, so this is totally inconsistent, contradictory to organise such activities in wartime, supposing that this was targeting civilians. This is also true for the famous water line because, there again, where are we? We are on an essential objective. So this is why such incidents cannot be qualified as attacks on civilians. Third shelling incident on Dobrinja, same reasoning. We are facing shelling incidents with an objective which is very close to the confrontation line. What I said earlier on holds true here as well. Sorry, let's move straight away to Alipasino Polje, same observation, same comments here as to this location. We know that there were two things. There was a unit with the mechanised and armoured material and assets. This is a well known fact, as the trial record shows. And there was also a military police units apparently that were based there. Now, back to Markale. This is the fifth shelling incident. Fifth scheduled shelling incident. But later on, I hasten to say, I will go back to all the other interesting shelling incidents in the Galic case. As far as Sarajevo is concerned, two preliminary remarks. First, the evidence of the number of cases, and also the issues of fragments or pieces, shards, shrapnels. Is it too fast for the interpreters? Is that okay? If it's too fast, I'll slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down a little bit, please, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems to be no protest, so I'll carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters would be thankful if the counsel would --

utterances.speaker: THE FRENCH INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We are requesting if the speaker could --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... the same position as you are, Mr. President. For once, we are not listening to the interpreters. I'll carry on. So let me come back to the Markale issue. There is first the proof by numbers as follows. How many proved shelling or shells were directed at Markale, of which it can be proved with certainty that there would have been established and acknowledged by specialist, by experts, as being shellings directed at the market and whose source of -- would have been proved? Look in the press, look in the trial record. You will find basically only one such case, and this is Markale. This is one single shell, whilst in the trial record you will find solid evidence showing that with 120-millimetre shells, I'm thinking of Witness AD, usually Serbs would fire twice and usually with twin tubes. So normally the two shells should have fallen at the same time on Markale, whilst there was only one. Secondly, fragments, and this is the most sensitive point in this whole issue, we know, and this is Exhibit D60, D61. This is a copy of documents disclosed by the Prosecution. We know that there were some 70 or 80 fragments or shrapnels of such shells that were all collected on site and very quickly, after the explosion, as is said in the trial record. These shrapnels exist because the Prosecution could touch them, could photograph them, could turn them into evidence, and when we asked for such documents, for material evidence to be produced, for the shrapnels to be produced, it's a miracle, wonder of it all, they had disappeared. This is a major trial on very serious crimes, and we wanted to check whether there was one shell, or two, or several, something we'll never know. Suddenly, all of a sudden, all these elements disappeared. And how do they disappear? You don't know. I don't know. Nobody will ever know. All that is said is that strangely enough, surprisingly enough, they are very sorry but they've lost them, so these are the most material pieces of evidence ever lost. Oh, no, no. They found the tail fin stabilising it. But when you do forensic examination on this, it cannot be contradictory to anything else because we have only one piece. To have a contradiction you need at least two pieces to make a comparison, and only the tail fin did not get lost. This is surprising. So whom is it serving? Is it serving justice, I wonder? And does justice serve the law if starting from evidence that is known to have existed they decide not to produce the evidence at court, in order for the Defence to be prevented from exercising its rights. This is the question respectively put to you by the Defence. Of course, we don't believe the story. The Defence do not believe that these documents, this evidence, would have gone missing, and the Defence submits that Markale could never be considered as evidence in the framework of a campaign of terror. I'm going to prove it. First, generally. There are many experts, as you are experts in law, as the Prosecution team is made of experts in law, but there are forensic experts but they have -- we have experts who were never able to agree. While they are very competent and reliable to know where the shell came from. This is quite peculiar. That a Trial Chamber could forensically pretend that and claim that they know more than experts whom themselves say that they don't know about it. Secondly, there are technical elements to it put forward by the Chamber, relying on just one thing, the angle of descent of the shell. Starting from that only, General Galic is going to be found guilty. I claim that this is a little thin, and I also claim that this is totally insufficient, and I'd like to prove this to you. Also, to answer one of the questions put by your Chamber. Firstly, the angle of descent of the shell. In order to see the flight path and the source of fire or the range of fire, and this is going to be considered applying two things: First, the Sandia Laboratory formula with regard to the theoretical penetration of the missile in the ground, and of course, secondly, the nature of the ground. These two predicates are essential to the reasoning. But in practical, these premises are wrong for the following ground. Firstly, the Trial Chamber totally neglected and failed to consider in its reasoning the possibility that another factor may have come into play. The roof or one of the roofs. If I say so, it is because there is D64, transcript 5416, in the trial record, there is a video recording where you hear at the very time of the incident somebody who says, and I quote by memory, "Go and look on the roof," whether there is -- there is not some shrapnels of the shell. Go and look on the roof. So why, at the time of the incident, that happened on the ground, would somebody have thought of going on -- to have a look on the roof to see what happened? This is a piece of evidence in the trial record. And I say, is it possible for a shell, when it falls, in an urban environment sort of hits a roof whilst falling? And you don't need to be an expert to understand that if you hit a roof when falling, without exploding it's going to change your trajectory, the flight path, and this should have been taken into consideration, or at least considered before being ruled out. This is my first ground. Second ground, which is very significant. The Trial Chamber, starting from the Sandia Laboratory formula, never in reality examined what the degree of resilience of the ground. They say it was made of bitumen and gravel, okay, fine, but if you go into the street and look at what's happened you'll see that in this very city where we are, there are city streets made of bitumen that are totally changed by the vehicles passing. So that does mean that the materials do not have the same level of resistance, and we should have conducted very precise research to know what was the degree of resilience to penetration of that particular piece of ground. Failing that, we were bound to make a mistake. I'll come back to this later. Other absolutely essential point. The Trial Chamber is perfectly right in noting that with regard to the craters the hole made by the shell, and this is judgement page -- it had -- [In English] "... redug in order to extract the tail fin." [Interpretation] This was paragraph 447. I also draw your attention to footnote 1618. Inevitably, the Trial Chamber should have concluded this: This crater had been destroyed or redug, widened and changed structurally in its very appearance before any steps could have been made. But you might say this is not that important. Well, I say yes. And I hope you will follow my demonstration. There is evidence showing a soldier sort of digging in the crater in order to try and find the tail fin. Well, three centimetres, Your Honours, it may be not much, it may be the thickness of my pencil here. Three centimetres in difference, in error. It's just the end of a knife. It's a gravel, a piece of gravel that jumps from the bottom of the crater. But an error of three to four centimetres, that might mean 33.4 per cent or more of error, of the standard of error. Because this crater allegedly was about nine centimetres deep. Look, if you have an error because the hole has been redug, you have an error of 33, or 45 per cent for four centimetres. The entire calculation is wrong, and who can guarantee to me that when this crater was redug, this did not happen? How did can we say today definitively that the crater remained unchanged? There is one piece of testimony coming from a witness who said yes, yes, this is the same tail fin, because when I took it and I put it back, I had no problem in putting it back into place. This is said by Mr. Zecvic, I believe. I'm just quoting him by memory. It was not difficult to put it back, he said. Fine. But if you have no problem putting it back, what does that mean? It means precisely that the crater had been changed in its width, in its depth so that it could be put back without any difficulty. So this is the very evidence that the hole had been changed, that it was impossible to take any further measurements following that change. Second point that seems important to me. The Trial Chamber relied on the principle that it could found its analysis on the American laboratory formula that I've quoted already, which determines the degree of penetration into a ground, so the initial speed that is necessary, and based on the initial speed, you can infer the range of fire. Fine, I say. But the Trial Chamber did not go as far as it should have gone if it really wanted to obtain reliable results because what is the question to be put actually? This is the real question. These technical data, formulas, and results how long have they been in existence, how long have they been available to the community, not the international legal community but the international community of experts? The Trial Chamber gives an answer but does not infer the necessary logical consequences. I now refer to footnote 1640, 1640, page 195 of the trial judgement. It says that the Berezansky formula is similar or analogous in its results to the American laboratory but it existed since the beginning of the 20th century. I repeat, since the beginning of the 20th century. So now the question is as follows: We know that there is a formula in existence since the beginning of the 20th century that provides analogous or similar results, and we also know that in Sarajevo, especially where this question really mattered, because this is what an urban environment where the lines criss-crossed, we know that this formula was never used by all of the community of technicians, experts and ballistics. Why was it not used? I'm going to tell you why. But I think there is only one answer to this question. It is because these formulas are not at all reliable. They are very theoretical, but in reality they are not reliable. If they were reliable, of course, experts in ballistics, technicians would have used them, and we would have long known where exactly the fire came. If you do not use those formulas, it is for the very reason that there is no consensus, no agreement about these formulas among the experts. If there is no agreement, it is because that's not the way it works in reality on the ground. The Trial Chamber and the Judges are not experts in ballistics. They could not do more than what all the technicians could do in this regard. Other elements regarding to the Markale incidents, and I would be thankful if in due time you looked at the French transcript. There is a piece of testimony that is absolutely decisive, and it really shows the innocence of General Galic. It is the testimony of Witness AK-1, paragraph 454 of the judgement. There again, the majority only did half of what it should have done. I'll explain what I mean. At the time I heard the witness, when that witness testified, I'm talking about Witness AK, and this is what he said, and unfortunately it was not to be found in the English transcript. That's why I'm asking to you look at the French transcript which is comprehensive, extensive and really matches what the witness said in their mother tongue. I was listening to the Serbo-Croat. I'm quoting now the French transcript. 15th of March, 2002, transcript page 5453. With regard to the shelling of the 5th of February, 1994, this is what the witness says. I quote: "And this is something that flew above us." 5453. A little further on, 5472: "I heard the shell, the noise made by the shell." And then something, as if it were something that was shooting above the house. Transcript 5472. Trial record. So we have a witness here who says, "I live 500 metres away from the Serbian lines in an area known to be hilly. I heard two things, he says. I heard the shelling, and she describes it as an exploding bottle and then something that flew above my house that I heard, and in court, she heard that as a whizzing sort of, and I think said [noise] or something like this, this kind of noise to indicate whizzing or a sign of sound as it flew above the house. So let's take the Trial Chamber's reasoning but in a reverse way, back to front. Look at the flight path. More or less 75 degrees from the departure point in the Defence views. Of course we left school long ago, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They know how much I like them and I shall comply with your wish. And with my apologies to them. We all remember our school-time, and we knew how to use a compass -- or we take an angle of 65 degrees, we project on the horizontal line the distance of 500 metres, and we take the vertical line. So if we have a 65-degree angle, I made the calculation, the distance in altitude is about 1.000 metres. I challenge -- I challenge, Your Honour, Your Honours, each and every one of us, how can -- to hear at an altitude of 1.000 metres, an object that is not self-propelled, that does not have an engine, that flies silently? I challenge each and every one of us to hear that noise. I'm not saying that the witness lied. Of course, he said the truth. But I say how can we try to understand what he said? How could he have heard the flight? He said it was a flight. There is a very simple answer to that. It was that the shell was flying much lower, as it flew over the house, and for it to fly much lower with allegedly an angle of 65 degrees, an acute angle, it must have been fired from much closer on. So much less than 500 metres, which is the distance within the witness's house and the confrontation line. In other words, the mere fact that this witness heard the object fly over his house, or her house, is the undisputable evidence. Unless you want to not see it, this is the finite evidence that this shell was fired from a distance from which it is possible to hear its flight. I mean, for a person in a house can hear its flight, and this is the evidence that this shell was not fired from the Serbian lines. But because the Trial Chamber did not try to find this testimony in the French transcript, the Trial Chamber missed an opportunity to declare Galic not guilty. You have to do it now. Now, about the silent object, we have clear evidence in the trial record, trial transcript 6228. Last point with regard to Markale. We are being told in so many words that this was intentional, that the mens rea has been established for General Galic, but if you have a look at the reasoning behind this mens rea, then something is very striking. What is very striking is the lack of arguments, the meagre arguments, put forward by the Trial Chamber. What are we being told? We are being told that a market is always likely to be hit, and because this marketplace was hit it was hit intentionally. I've summed up the reasoning of the Chamber but if you read it again, you will see that it's exactly what I'm telling you. There were a lot of people on the marketplace; therefore, it was an interesting target. Does this mean that I will necessarily destroy it? We are being told that the Serbs were very good at firing on positions and that's why they fired on this position, and we are being told that General Galic wanted to hit that marketplace but we don't know why. On the other hand, in the judgement, the exculpatory evidence is never being considered, including the evidence given by Witness AD, a man who told us that they always fired salvo of two shells at the same time. And as far as I know, in Markale, the Prosecution always said that there was just one single shell that hit the marketplace. If I was to make a reference to decisions older than the motu Morales [phoen] decision, the famous decisions that is not going to be very useful to us today, I will say the following: [No interpretation]. Now, let's move on to your second question, Mr. President. I don't know if the interpreters have understood. Well, the interpreters state that they do not interpret from Latin on a regular basis. Mr. President, let me go back to your question, the second question on the Scheduling Order. There are two ways of answering your question. The first option is to examine, to review very quickly, all the paragraphs of the Trial Chamber judgement showing us that these attacks cannot be seen as deliberate attacks. And the second option is statistics, a statistical object, statistical answer. Let me list very quickly the paragraphs of the judgement I want to review. To make the job of the interpreters easier, I will tell you what these paragraphs are and then I will review them one after the other. These are paragraphs 210, 212, 213, 215, 218, 216, 219, 220, 222, 222 -- 220, 222, 229, 231, 234, 244, [In English] 292, 322, 325, 328, 329, 368, 370, 414, 417, 435, 436 and 562. [Interpretation] These are the paragraphs we'll review in detail, Mr. President. 210. These are general comments without any specification. This can't be verified, and this is contradiction with Exhibit 3137, P3137, the report of Mrs. Tabeau. 212. General Briquemont is quoted but unfortunately what is not quoted here is what he himself stated and as follows: [In English] "How do you want to avoid the shelling of the city of Sarajevo." [Interpretation] Transcript 10100. 213. Let me quote the judgement: "The Defence repeatedly proposed to witnesses who served the UN in Sarajevo that the physical damage was greater on the front line than in the city, implying that the casualties inflicted in the city were unintentional. The trial record shows however that there was more shelling going into the city and that civilians, and the civilian population as such, in ABiH-held areas of Sarajevo were targeted from SRK-controlled territory." This is completely wrong. This is a serious mistake, a serial factual mistake, Mr. President. Let me quote Mandilovic, 7th of December, 2001, transcript 1054. Let me quote him. [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] "In the south part of the city. [Interpretation] Hammer, 16th of May, 2002, 8526 on the transcript, about shelling, hitting areas close to commanding posts. [Previous translation continues] ... "near the confrontation line or military installation, yes." [Interpretation] Major Henneberry, a witness who found it a good idea to talk to another witness in order to refresh his memory. We watch and report Muslims shell airport from Mount Igman, Ilidza. (Again the news reports were wrong and the wrong side took the blame internationally for actions they didn't start)." [Interpretation] Tucker, 18th of June, 2002, transcript 10032. Michael Rose, 20th of June, 2002, transcript 10261, he says the following [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] "... 94 appeared close to the line of conflict that is so." [Interpretation] Witness Y, 1st of July, 2002, transcript 10941. He's very clear, although in closed session, and then General Adrianus Van Baal, a Dutch man, transcript 11381: [In English] "I would like us to focus on Sarajevo. Could you first confirm if this is the case since we have had some testimony to this effect? That the major destructions occurred in the area of the demarcation line on or the confrontation line?" "Answer: That's correct."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm trying. Paragraph 215 of the judgement, 215 and 218. With respect to shellings, nothing of what Ashton said should have been considered. This witness is not reliable, not credible. If you look at all the journalists in the world, you can see that he's the only one who was never transferred to an American base in Sarajevo and then -- so he's the only one who benefitted from this treatment without having to pay a penny for it as opposed to the other journalises. And just as Judge Nieto-Navia understood what it was all about, we all understood what it was all about. Please refer to page 24 of the dissenting opinion of Judge Nieto-Navia. Paragraph 216. [In English] "...not to attack civilians." [Interpretation] Quoting from memory: [In English] "...attack civilians." [Interpretation] Well, in English as well as in French it means that you have to abstain not to attack civilians, in other words, you have to attack them. This is a lapsus calami. As for Witness AD, please look at transcript 10755. Paragraph 220, Mr. Hvaal, testimony of Mr. Hvaal never corroborated. Paragraph 222. [In English] "... rarely leaving their apartment. [Interpretation] This is in contradiction with -- to paragraph 216. And now let me review neighbourhood by neighbourhood. 229, Grbavica area. Paragraph 231. Once again, and this is something that occurs throughout the judgement, we have no specifications about the shellings. That would have allowed to us say, no, this is in relation with the specific attack or strategy. 244, Ashton again, nothing specific about the shellings. 245, same thing. We do not even know if the damage described here occurred during the period, the commanding period, or outside of that period. 246, Hrasno. Yes, he gave dates but why didn't Mr. Ierace provide the specific examples to the Tribunal? 292, Alipasino Polje. No specific information about the shellings. Nedzarici is mentioned, but the Trial Chamber does not say that Nedzarici was razed by -- Nedzarici was razed by non-Serb shellings. Then the following paragraph, a balcony that was destroyed but it is not mentioned that it was on the separation line. 328, 329, Butmir, Igman, but Butmir and Igman were not Serbian positions. Dobrinja, 368, same thing with regard to what is stated by UN personnel we have no idea if this refers to a previous period or not. 369. Another balcony has been destroyed but this is a different line of confrontation. 370, Dobrinja again. Divided into two parts. It's true that the place was shelled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, I have to interrupt you. You have to slow down a bit for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's obvious that I haven't been at the Tribunal for quite sometime. I'll try. I'll do my best. I'll try to slow down. 370. Dobrinja was the area with the most -- highest level of conflicts but Nedzarici is not mentioned. Nedzarici, the Serb area that was razed to the ground. Then 374, the -- about the airports. The Trial Chamber does not record that the airport was not fired upon. Then Brdo, usually a military objective. Stari Grad, Markale, here again the Trial Chamber states that it has been hit by Serb firing, but the old brewery was -- is mentioned, but it was not -- what's not mentioned is that everybody knew that it was a storage place, and it was an area where arms were being repaired. Therefore, a military objective, legitimate objectives. What is not stated is that the Bistric barracks were located there with Commander Cacak [phoen]. 562. That's the last paragraph I'm going to mention to answer your question. Here, the Trial Chamber has omitted to take into account that after the 5th of February 1994, no shelling is possible anymore. Why? First of all, because firing has stopped and also because heavy weaponry, thanks to General Galic, who executed that, as part of the total exclusion zone, the heavy weaponry is being removed to an area located 20 kilometres away from Sarajevo. So whatever is being said, no campaign of shelling is possible from the beginning of 1994. Mr. President, I'm now going to move on to the second part of my demonstration, but for that I will need the ELMO - I suppose you still have an ELMO in the courtrooms - and I will need the assistance of the usher. I'd like her to place this document on the ELMO, with your permission. Sorry, please -- can you please wait? I've got a number of documents I would like to show you. And the copies will be given to the Prosecution. Your Honour, I don't know if I'll be granted additional time since we have some slight technical hiccups here. Things are not going as quickly as I thought they would. Can everybody see the document on the monitor? Yes, Mr. President. This is a document from the Prosecution. It's a page from Mrs. Tabeau's report. Can you please show the entire page. I'm mostly interested in the graph. I'd like to see the page -- yeah, the bottom of the page. Okay. Let me take the example of Stari Grad, just as an example. The light area, for females, it's not relevant in terms of numbers, but as for males, the light part indicates civilians and the dark coloured area indicates or represents the military. We have taken the example of Stari Grad that everybody presents as purely civilian area. We have a military population of 45 to -- 40 to 45.000 people, for a total population of 340.000. With this supposedly indiscriminate shelling on the supposedly civilian area, we have four times more military casualties than civilian casualties. And since the ratio was one-to-seven, seven times more civilians than military personnel, to arrive at that result of four times more military casualties, we have to multiply all this by seven. In other words, in this supposedly civilian area, you had 30 times more -- I'm not talking about 30 per cent, I'm saying that there were 30 times more military casualties than civilian casualties. These are the figures of the Prosecution. These are not our figures. Under these circumstances, how can you say that there were no selective and proportionate fires? And to finish - you can leave that on the ELMO - let me go back to your last question. If terror existed, the crime of terror exists, and we've always stated that that's not the case, if that exists, can it be implemented by fire on legitimate, on lawful objectives but without respect of the principle of proportionality? Under those circumstances, could terror ensue? I understand what you're aiming at in order to possibly modify, alter the judgement. Let me say that Sarajevo is not the laboratory we need, because in Sarajevo there are many, many targets. These targets are legitimate, as in other cities. When you fire on such a target in the city, those who live around the targets, after the first explosion - and this, it's quite normal, they are civilians - they will feel terror, which is quite normal, legitimate. Terror is something that a civilian will experience when a bomb explodes. Terror there exists, and if proportion -- the principle of proportionality had not been complied with, then we can say that right from the beginning, there was terror in Sarajevo due to the legitimate use of force as part of these operations. So we come to the question of whether it's possible to murder a dead man. That's basically what it comes down to here, and the answer obviously is no. Therefore, you cannot create a legitimate and lawful terror by not respecting the principle of proportionality. Why not? Why not? It's because in Sarajevo, if the -- if a legitimate targets had been identified, and that was never done, and if you distinguish between illegitimate and legitimate actions, in Sarajevo, terror was the result of legitimate, lawful actions. Therefore, you cannot imagine anything else in Sarajevo. I'm finished, Mr. President. Therefore, let me say that a yes answer cannot be given to your question. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The second part of the question put to the Defence asks that we answer the fact what were those direct attacks that were wrongly categorised by the Trial Chamber that led to erroneous conclusions? The Defence has to point out that it was established that in the course of the conflict, on the Sarajevo front, there were legitimate military actions. This is what the OTP acknowledged themselves, and the OTP was supposed to separate those that were legitimate from those that were not. And they failed to do that. The scheduled incidents during the trial changed. So in addition to scheduled incidents, which were submitted together with the second addendum to the indictment, where the Prosecutor put on a certain incident, no other incidents were reviewed. The Defence would now like to point your attention to paragraph 86 of the Expert Commission of the United Nation where it is stated that in order to establish whether an incident was non-legitimate or not, what needs to be established was both the time of that operation, the geographic location, the position of the parties, and all other circumstances. When deciding whether there were direct attacks on civilians and whether there was a crime of terror, the Trial Chamber did not establish a single fact in relation to these factors, such as the place and time of the action, the position, deployment of the parties, and the capacity of victims. The Trial Chamber relies erroneously on the so-called general evidence. The Defence believes that such erroneous findings of the Trial Chamber about direct attacks on civilians is based both on errors in fact and errors in law because the Trial Chamber inferred such findings on the basis of the so-called general evidence. We would like to draw your attention to paragraph 188 of the judgement - we are now dealing with general evidence - where the Trial Chamber itself devotes attention to evaluating certain evidence, namely the distance between the victim and the most likely source of fire, the distance between the place where the victims was hit and the confrontation line, combat operations which were taking place at the time, relevant presence of military activities and facilities in the vicinity, the appearance of the victims, how visible the victim was and how the victim was dressed, as well as the ability of unobstructed line of sight. The Defence claims that whether it comes to the so-called unscheduled incidents, the Trial Chamber did not go into any of these elements because, simply speaking, the witnesses of the Prosecution, in their evidence, didn't provide a single valid fact based on which these elements could be analysed. Thus, the Trial Chamber, when it comes to a direct attack on civilians, came to an erroneous conclusion. Another portion of the reasoning in paragraph 188 of the judgement shows that the Trial Chamber also erred when it stated that, in accordance with the law set out in part 2 of this judgement and in fairness to the accused, the Trial Chamber had to decide whether a scheduled incident is beyond reasonable doubt representative of the alleged campaign of sniping and shelling or whether it is reasonable to believe, which was very important, that the victim was hit by ABiH forces, by a stray bullet, or taken for a combatant. And the forces of ABiH were also targeting civilians. Thus we have to wonder, how was it possible for the Trial Chamber to come to this general conclusion that there was a direct attack on civilians as part of a campaign in part of all other cases, not only in scheduled incidents, when the Trial Chamber did not go into analysing a single incident? The Trial Chamber dealt with this in paragraphs 582 to 595 of the judgement. By failing to establish facts in all unscheduled incidents, the Trial Chamber, in our view, founded its conclusions on assumptions, because when looking at scheduled incidents and establishing that such a small number of these scheduled incidents was actually representative of the entire campaign. My apologies. Now the Defence would like to go into analysing scheduled incidents. When it comes to scheduled incidents, it is our position that the Trial Chamber only in these instances analysed the issues that I referred to in the introduction to my presentation. The Defence would -- believes that the Trial Chamber wrongly categorised these direct attacks on civilians as the alleged attacks in all scheduled incidents, and concluded erroneously that this could be attributed to General Galic. In our view, it cannot be attributed to any single member of the SRK let alone General Galic, and we support this view by pointing to the consistent evidence of Defence witnesses as well as various expert witnesses who relied on state-of-the-art scientific evidence. I have to point to the fact that in the indictment, the OTP referred to 32 scheduled incidents of sniper attack and six incidents of shelling throughout the 23 months of the indictment, and the first incident was ten months before the arrival of General Galic to the post of corps commander. The Prosecution added five new incidents, and in those five new incidents, they also included an incident which took place on the 13th of December, 1992. When it comes to shelling incidents, the first was on the 1st of June. The Defence wonders whether when it comes to a period before December 1992, that is to say a period of more than three months, we wonder what about the period of ten months before the 1st of June, 1993, when allegedly the first deliberate shelling of civilians took place? These ten months of the alleged representative sample of the campaign and more than three months without representative sniping of civilians, these are all periods of time that contradict the finding of the majority that there was a campaign of deliberate attack on civilians. Judge Rodrigues issued a ruling on the 5th of October, 2001, denying them the ability to analyse facts and stating that that can be used only as an illustration, and this could be done only in order to establish unlawfulness of somebody's conduct. This change in attitude points to the fact that the Prosecution could not prove in these ten incidents that were withdrawn that there was a deliberate attack on civilians, which confirms the position of the Defence, that it is impossible to conclude that such an incident was a deliberate targeting of civilians. So the trial began with 26 sniping incidents and five shelling incidents. After the Prosecution concluded their case, when the Defence asked for acquittal claiming that the OTP failed to prove the existence of crimes, the Trial Chamber acquitted him in relation to three incidents, 7, 12 and 19. And the position of the Trial Chamber was that the evidence led in relation to incidents 7, 12 and 19 wasn't sufficient to convince them beyond a reasonable doubt that the soldiers under command and control of General Galic conducted a direct attack on civilians. After the Defence case, the Trial Chamber concluded that additional five scheduled incidents were not proven by the Prosecution; 13, 21, 11, 14 and 26. Therefore, out of 23 scheduled incidents, based on the position of the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution didn't prove five of them, a total of eight, three of which were mentioned in the acquittal, 98 bis ruling, and five in the judgement. So the Trial Chamber established that only eight incidents were proven. And the majority believed that ten were proven. Judge Navia in his opinion believed that ten were not proven. Without analysing the opinion of Judge Navia, the Defence would like to point out that out of 26 incidents which -- concerning which evidence were led, eight were by ruling of majority found as unproven and eight were, which is to say that this is one-third or 33.33 per cent of scheduled evidence. The majority believed that these 18 incidents were representative of the campaign of deliberate targeting of civilians aimed at spreading terror, whereas Judge Navia did not accept this conclusion. He thought that this was not representative of the campaign but, rather, that these were isolated attacks on civilians. The conclusion is that the scheduled incidents cannot be representative of the general situation in Sarajevo. Not only that, they can't be even representative of the direct attack on civilians, and we shall be speaking further when we come to the analysis of scheduled sniping incidents. Given the analysis that we just presented to you, and which was described in paragraph 188 of the judgement, and when analysing the reasons that the Trial Chamber described, these reasons would boil down to the following: Impossibility to reconstruct the events; inconsistency in the evidence of witnesses when it comes to incident 16 and 2; possibility to injure a victim through a ricochet or stray bullet, incident 5, 24, 20, 23 and 4; unreliable nature of establishing the source of the bullet in incidents 7, 2, 15, 18 and so on; and unreliability of information on the position of the victim, weather and visibility and distance, and possibility to discern whether the victim was a civilian or a soldier, incidents 10, 20, 27 and 18; vicinity of military -- or, rather, the fact that military facilities were close, such as soldiers, canteens, military check-points and so on; unreliability of panoramic photographs, as well as the features of the place where the alleged victim was, whether it was an isolated place on the hills, a forest where one doesn't expect to come across civilians and so on. Based on this, the Trial Chamber rejected incidents 13, 21, 26, 11 and 14 in their ruling, and in their ruling on the 3rd of October, 2002, they rejected incidents 7, 12 and 19. The Defence, in addition to the above reasons, will now also point to the reasons which exclude direct and deliberate attack on civilians in the remaining scheduled sniping incidents. This was my response to the second part of the question, and in view of the limited time, in relation to all of these nine elements listed in paragraph 188 of the judgement, I also listed the incidents that could fall under this item 9. And by applying these standards, all of these incidents, that is to say these 18 incidents, were in view of the majority representative can be thus rejected. Thus, by failing to apply identical standards and by applying the reasons of the majority in a smaller number of incidents, the Trial Chamber erroneously made conclusions about these scheduled incidents that I just listed. However, we provided a detailed analysis of all of these incidents in our appeals brief. And by going outside of its standards, the Trial Chamber drew wrong conclusions about deliberate targeting of civilians. The attacks on civilians, even if proven, cannot be sufficient to establish that there was a pattern. Because if we take into account the fact that the front line was 27 kilometres long, one can only come to a reasonable conclusion that these were isolated events, where due to the situation prevailing on the front some civilians got hurt, yes. I also have to point out that the Trial Chamber should have been guided by the principle in dubio pro reo as we stated in paragraph 16 of our brief, which is what Judge Navia stated in his opinion in paragraph 10. The majority was duty-bound to look for intent, and the intent was not proven in any scheduled or unscheduled incidents based on which the Trial Chamber should have rejected these incidents, especially by relying on the principle of in dubio pro reo as one of the basic principles of criminal law. By failing to do that, the Trial Chamber concluded that there was an intentional targeting of civilians which is an erroneous conclusion. They concluded that this deliberate targeting of civilians was aimed at spreading terror. This intent, which includes the deliberate attack of civilians, is something that the Prosecutor didn't even try to prove, and they didn't prove it ultimately. And here we draw your attention to the report of expert witness Kuljic. As the analysis of my colleague, Piletta-Zanin, has proven that there was no indiscriminate shelling of civilians, we stand by the position that the same is true of sniping incidents. Because when firing from a light weaponry, it can -- this type of firing can only be -- cannot be discriminate. And here we refer you to a report of the Security Council of United Nations, paragraph 6(B). The inability to establish the distance and the possibility of establishing visual line of sight from the place where one is firing from and the place where there is victim, it is impossible under those circumstances to conclude whether this was deliberate targeting of that particular target or not. Especially I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that during the trial, it was proven that the members of Sarajevo-Romanija Corps did not have any snipers. In addition to that, in no incident was it determined who actually fired the shot, so it is impossible to prove beyond a reasonable doubt -- or to conclude beyond reasonable doubt that a member of SRK actually fired the shots. It would be possible to only assume, but that is not a basis for a conclusion of fact or law. I would also like to stress that had the Trial Chamber visited the site and visited -- and been able to see the topographic features and the position where the bullet was fired and the -- where the victim actually stood and whether there was a line of sight, had that been done, it would have been able to make such conclusions whether there was an intent to fire on civilians at all. So the Trial Chamber erred, the majority erred, when it decided there was a deliberate campaign to spread terror among civilians because neither the direct attacks nor such intent have been actually proven. Now we would like to answer the question, in the question number 3, as to the length of time in which the hospital remains a legitimate military target after the end of military activities. The Defence has to say that this is only a hypothetical question, not a specific question, because the Prosecution did not prove and could not prove the attack of SRK forces on any hospital, so we don't have any time of targeting from the hospital and of the hospital. The majority dealt only with the Kosevo hospital in paragraph 509, concluding that the hospital building was fired, and also referring to the estimates of damage to Kosevo hospital done by Prosecution expert, Mr. Harding. I have to also stress that this was not actually the Kosevo hospital but the military hospital. We have to stress that Kosevo hospital was never -- there were no impacts on the Kosevo hospital itself. There were only impacts in the yard of the hospital held by the ABiH units, on the firing positions that they had there. The firing positions were identified in the hospital compound, and whenever fire was opened from those positions, SRK members fired back, and in that -- in those conditions, the hospital was a legitimate military target. DP-51, Defence witness, explained that throughout the time that he worked in the hospital, there were three tanks positioned in the hospital compound and three combat vehicles. The Defence would like to note also the protest admitted into evidence as Defence Exhibit D29, sent by General Morillon to Alija Izetbegovic, noting that mortars were firing from the Kosevo hospital, and this is a repeated protest. Also, Mr. Carswell mentioned -- General -- Mr. Carswell mentioned that at least 25 -- he received information that the hospital was used to fire shells and to attack SRK forces. Also, testimony by Witness Tucker, assistant aide de camp of General Morillon from October 1992 to March 1993, where he notes that ABiH troops were opening fire from the hospital. In accordance with the Geneva Conventions, the hospital thus becomes a legitimate target without any temporal limitations because three tanks and APCs were actually located there. The Defence would also like to refer to page 144, annex 6 of the expert, UN Expert Commission report, where it says that from May until December, eight months before the appointment of General Galic as the SRK commander, that the hospital was targeted also in that -- eight times was targeted in that period. The Defence believes that it is impossible to actually answer to the question asked by the Appeals Chamber as to how long a hospital remains a legitimate military target after the end of the military activities from the hospital. The question is how much time has to elapse for a military operation to be considered as completed and for the other side, the opposite party, to be convinced that there will be no further military action from a certain position? So this is the response of the Defence regarding question 5. As regards the answer of the Defence to the question as to why we believe that the Trial Chamber erred when it decided not to take the on-site visit, we believe that it would have been in the interests of justice and very useful for the full and proper determination of facts, it would have been in the interests of justice for the Trial Chamber -- had the Trial Chamber visited the site of the incidents and to find out firsthand what they look like and to be able to determine the distance from the place where the bullet was fired to where the victim actually stood, whether there were any obstructions in the line of sight. We believe that it would have been most useful had the Trial Chamber visited the sites after the -- both the Prosecution and the Defence had rested their case, because they would have been able to see for themselves and to give appropriate value to the evidence presented by the both parties. And the Trial Chamber would have been able to determine that the SRK did not control the high positions around the town, the town of Sarajevo.

Does the fact of confirming an indictment and subsequently of sitting at the trial of the -- of the accused, whose indictment he has confirmed, reflect the Judge's bias? This is the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for asking this, Your Honour. I will have to give you some explanation. Can I do so? Yes, thank you. Yes, I will answer in the affirmative, inasmuch as the proceeding or the procedure of confirming, which is known and applied by this Tribunal, implies two things: Firstly, that a case file will be disclosed, which the Defence will not have, will not be appraised of. And secondly, the fact that the Judge will have ruled as to the possible existence of the guilt of somebody on the basis of prima facie evidence. What I say is the following: If you have a Judge, such as Presiding Judge Orie, who on the basis of prima facie holds that the evidence produced by the Prosecution in the Mladic case cannot be reversed by any Defence, there is good cause to allege genocide, and therefore, that genocide would then be established, and if the active participation of General Galic is mentioned, it means that the said Judge admitted in this hypothesis but officially and publicly that General Galic committed acts of genocide within the consideration of prima facie evidence. So I answer yes. And this shows the bias you mentioned. Why so? Because we know that in all legal systems an accused must objectively consider from a subjective point of view but must objectively consider that the Judge who is going to try him will not be biased. However, in this case, how an accused prosecuted for murder or crimes against humanity can imagine even if he knows that Judges are specialists that the Judge is going to be unbiased, when the said Judge, on the basis of a case file not known to the Defence, has already said yes, very clearly on the basis of prima facie, yes, that General Galic also committed acts of genocide. The crime of genocide is more serious than that of murder. This being so, it is obvious that any possibility of acquittal would be ruled out anywhere in the world. So I answer yes to your question. Thank you.

utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. What I'd like to do is just give a brief introduction, a brief outline as to how the Prosecution will proceed today in responding to the Defence's appeal. So with that outline in mind, I'll give the floor to Ms. Michelle Jarvis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. For his role, the majority convicted General Galic for the crime of terror and the Prosecution submits that the majority was correct in this conclusion. In support of this position, I'll address Your Honours today on five primarily legal issues in the following order: First, and in response to the first question that Your Honours have addressed to the Prosecution, I'll explain why the majority was correct to convict General Galic of terror based on the 22 May 1992 agreement that the parties had entered into, and in that same regard, why Article 3 of the Statute is broad enough to encompass jurisdiction over such international agreements. Second, and by way of an update to the Prosecution's response brief, I'll address the Chamber on the support that is derived from the 2005 ICRC customary law study for the classification of the crime of terror as part of customary international law. Third, and in response to the second question that Your Honours have addressed to the Prosecution, I'll explain why indiscriminate attacks against civilians can be regarded as part of the crime of terror. Fourth --

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Before I move on to discuss these legal issues, a brief factual context. The legal issues in this case are important because of the factual context in which they arise, because of the experiences of the civilian men, women and children of Sarajevo when General Galic commanded the SRK forces. What happened to the civilians of Sarajevo was something quite distinct and quite apart from the suffering and distress that inevitably accompanies armed conflict. The civilians of Sarajevo, in ABiH-controlled areas, were relentlessly and notoriously pursued as targets of the SRK shelling and sniping campaign. As one witness, an ABiH soldier, put it at paragraph 586 of the judgement, he felt safer at the front line in Sarajevo than anywhere else. I refer Your Honours to the judgement at paragraphs 584 to 585, finding that civilians were targeted during funerals, in ambulances, on trams, they were targeted during cease-fires, they were targeted when fetching water. They were targeted while shopping in marketplaces. Children were targeted in schools, playing outside, riding bicycles. Why were civilians targeted? Well, the siege of Sarajevo was witnessed by many international military and other observers who came before the Trial Chamber, one after another, to tell exactly what they had seen. These were neutral and experienced observers who knew exactly what they were witnessing. For all of these observers, caught within the amphitheatre of horror that Sarajevo became during the war, the deliberateness of the terror was palpable. Civilians were targeted because the SRK was carrying out psychological warfare on civilians to force a capitulation of the enemy. I'll play now for the Chamber some short extracts of the testimonies of six such witnesses. The corresponding transcript pages to the clips that I'll play for you today have been collated and copies have been made available for Your Honours, for the Defence and, for the Legal Officers. Even just a small sampling much these testimonies that I'll play for you now ring out this constant refrain.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: "One would very often get the impression that these people, you know, the pattern of these sniper incidents were people having, you know, a fairly morbid kind of fun with this. People would be frightened, you know. They would wait for somebody to cross a street, fire at the first people, not fire at the second person, fire close to people to make them turn around and run back, fire at water cans that were sitting in an intersection that had been dropped by someone, and then people would go out, try to hit -- you know, try to pick up the water can. You know, there would be bullets impacting around it or in it." "The impression that we gained was that the purpose of the shelling was in order to intimidate, firstly, the population of Sarajevo in general, and to break their will to resist, and secondly, in order to intimidate the Presidency of Alija Izetbegovic and break their will to resist." "I am personally certain of that, and that it was for well-calculated psychological reasons, to have a psychological impact on the local populace." "Could you tell us a little more of what that psychological impact objective was, in your opinion?" "To terrorise the local civilians and Muslim forces to make them on edge all the time, causing distress, lack of sleep, lack of will, especially, to carry on, lack of support for the Muslim cause, if I may use that, a standard psychological response in the sense of psychological warfare. On the civilian side, the impact of the psychological warfare application was working. They were indeed terrorised and on edge. "And in my view, the direct follow-on, the logical follow-on is that they were using it as an instrument of terror against the opposing side." "As far as the local population is concerned, the objective was clear, is to create a climate of terror, an atmosphere of terror, in the centre of the city, to make people feel on the edge." "The objectives were basically civilians in order to put pressure on the population." I'll turn, then, Your Honours, to the first issue in my arguments today and that is that the majority was right to convict General Galic for the crime of terror under Article 3 of Statute based on a prohibition set out in a clearly applicable international agreement. As I've mentioned, the basis for General Galic's conviction for the crime of terror was the special agreement entered into by the parties to the conflict in Bosnia on 22 May 1992. The Chamber found that it was unnecessary for it to inquire separately into the existence of the crime of terror as part of customary international law. Your Honours have asked the Prosecution to explain how Article 3 of this Tribunal's Statute can extend to such international agreements in light of comments that the Secretary-General made in his report on the Rwanda Tribunal. In particular, Your Honours have noted that in this report on the Rwanda Tribunal, the Secretary-General stated that the Security Council has elected to take a more expansive approach to the choice of applicable law than the one underlying the Statute of the Yugoslav Tribunal and included within the subject matter jurisdiction of the Rwanda Tribunal, international instruments regardless of whether they were part of customary international law. How does the Prosecution reconcile this statement with its position on Article 3 of this Tribunal? The short answer is that to the extent that the Secretary-General's statement in the ICTR report suggests that the jurisdiction of this Tribunal doesn't extend to such treaty provisions, it is not determinative because it is inconsistent with the plain wording of the Statute, also the comments of the Member States of the Security Council at the time that the Statute was adopted, and it's inconsistent with the object and purpose behind the establishment of this Tribunal. The Appeals Chamber has already reached similar conclusions in the Tadic jurisdiction Appeal judgement and the Kordic Appeal judgement. I'll briefly address these three issues, or subpoints, as I will refer to them. My first subpoint, the plain meaning of Article 3 of the Statute. This is the first step in interpreting the scope of Article 3, to look at the plain meaning of the words in that Article in light of the context of the Statute as a whole. This approach to statutory interpretation has been confirmed by the Appeals Chamber in several cases. And just by way of example, the Tadic Appeal judgement at paragraph 282; and the Celebici Appeal judgement at paragraph 68. What does the plain wording of Article 3 reveal? As the Tadic jurisdiction Appeals Chamber concluded at paragraph 87, the plain wording of Article 3 reveals that it covers a broad category of offences, namely all violations of the laws or customs of war and that the enumeration set out in Article 3 is illustrative, not exhaustive. Judge Sidhwa, at paragraph 113 of his separate opinion in the Tadic jurisdiction appeal decision, expressed the view that the ordinary meaning of the term "laws of war" are those set down in treaty provisions or other written documents and that the customs of war equate to customary international law drawn from state practice and opinio juris. Certainly the term "violations of the laws or customs of war" on its shorthand version, "violation of the laws of war," is generally understood as extending to the laws of war laid down in both in custom and treaty. For example, the military manual of Great Britain, which is set out in Leslie Green's book and contained in our supplementary book of authorities, this military manual states that: "The laws of war consist, partly of customary rules which have grown up in practice, and partly of written rules, that is to say, rules which have expressly been agreed upon by governments in international treaties and conventions." Similarly, the Encyclopaedia of Public and International Law, the Max Planck Institute published under their auspices, this is also in our book of authorities states that: "... the laws of war derive first and foremost from custom ... and ... treaties." The Kordic appeals Chamber found further support for the conclusion that Article 3 includes criminal prohibitions set out in treaty provisions in the wording of Article 1 of the Statute. At paragraph 43, the Kordic Appeals Chamber emphasised that the jurisdiction of this Tribunal extends to all serious violations of international humanitarian law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia.
