In sum, then, as to my first subpoint, the plain wording of Article 3 viewed in the context of the Statute as a whole is broad enough to extend to all serious violations of the laws or customs of war regardless of their source, whether that's treaty law or customary law. My second subpoint is that Security Council records confirm that member states adopting the Statute intended that Article 3 would cover international agreements. The case law of this Tribunal has recognised that, in addition to the plain wording of the Statute, the interpretive statements of states at the time the Statute was adopted can serve as a supplementary means of interpretation. Even if there was any confusion about the plain wording of Article 3, the record of the comments made by members of the Security Council when they adopted the Statute puts it beyond any doubt that applicable treaty provisions were intended to be covered. In fact, the members of the Security Council were at some pains to make this expressly clear. Why was it necessary for the members to emphasise this point in their comments? It was because the Secretary-General's 3 May 1993 report in which he set out his proposal for the Statute of the Tribunal stated that in order to comply with the principle of nullum crimen sine lege the Statute should extend only to violations of humanitarian law that are recognised as customary law. A few weeks after the Secretary-General submitted this report, the Security Council met to discuss the report and they adopted the Statute. They then made statements explaining their vote, and these statements clarified that the Member States understood Article 3 to specifically include treaty provisions binding the parties in the former Yugoslavia. Consider, in particular, Your Honours the statement made by the delegation from the United States of America which is contained in the verbatim record of the Security Council proceedings on that day and set out in our supplementary book of authorities. The delegate emphasised that she wanted to clarify clearly and completely the understandings that underpinned her government's support for the adoption of the Statute. She emphasised that while the Security Council had adopted the Statute as proposed by the Secretary-General, the report raised several technical issues that the US wanted to address through interpretive statements. The delegate underscored her view that the -- underscored the US government's view that their position on these clarifications were shared by other members of the council and, in particular, I quote, she said: "Firstly, it is understood that the laws or customs of war referred to in Article 3 include all obligations under humanitarian law agreements in force in the territory of the former Yugoslavia at the time the acts were committed, including common Article 3 of the 1949 Geneva Conventions and the 1977 Additional Protocols." No delegation contradicted these statements by the US government. Two other countries, the United Kingdom and France, both also made express statements clarifying that Article 3 must extend to applicable international agreements. The Appeals Chamber has reviewed these statements by members of the Security Council previously and has come to precisely this conclusion. I point Your Honours to the Tadic jurisdiction appeal decision, paragraphs 75, 88 and 143, and the Kordic appeal judgement at paragraph 43. The Prosecution acknowledges that the case law of this Tribunal has accepted that the report of the Secretary-General had been consulted to provide guidance when clarifying the Statute. However, the Prosecution submits that where the Member States of the Security Council expressly departed from comments made by the Secretary-General, their interpretive statements must prevail. In his report on the Rwanda Tribunal, it would have been correct for the Secretary-General to state that he had proposed a broader approach for the Rwanda Tribunal than the one that he had proposed for this Tribunal. But it was not the case that the Security Council had taken a broader approach. The Security Council took fundamentally the same approach for both Tribunals. The Prosecution agrees, though, that the concern underlying the Secretary-General's proposal to limit the jurisdiction of this Tribunal to customary law norms is a valid one. Article 3 cannot be interpreted in a way that would violate fundamental principles of justice, such as the principle of nullum crimen sine lege. But as this Chamber has held in both the Tadic jurisdiction Appeal Judgments and the Kordic Appeal judgement, accepting clearly applicable treaty provisions as a jurisdictional basis for Article 3 fully complies with nullum crimen concerns. Indeed, as the Appeals Chamber noted, at paragraph 41 of the Ojdanic joint criminal enterprise appeal decision of 21 May 2003, written law will often be more accessible to an accused person than customary law. Nullum crimen concerns don't warrant the exclusion of written law. I turn to my third subpoint and that is a very brief one, namely that to exclude clearly applicable treaty provisions would frustrate the intention of the Security Council that Article 3 be read broadly and it would -- and to thereby impunity or for all serious violations of applicable humanitarian law norms. The fundamental preoccupation underlying the statements of virtually all of the Security Council Member States when they adopted the Statute was the catastrophic consequences of according impunity to persons who have violated international humanitarian law. These statements are amply reflected in the verbatim record which, as I've mentioned, is included as part of our supplementary book of authorities. In conclusion to my argument on the scope of Article 3 of the Statute, the Appeals Chamber has already repeatedly confirmed that clearly applicable treaty provisions are covered by Article 3. To depart from these holdings would require cogent reasons. The comment of the Secretary-General in the context of the Rwanda statute does not provide cogent reasons. The Appeals Chamber in Tadic jurisdiction and in Kordic fully took into account that the Secretary-General's view was that the Tribunal's jurisdiction should be limited to customary law norms. The Appeals Chamber rightly found on both those occasions that this statement was not determinative and that the plain wording of the Statute and the understanding and the comments of the Security Council Member States should prevail. The Secretary-General's reiteration of his view in the ICTR report does not add anything new or change the conclusion that should be reached. I'll turn now, Your Honours, to the second legal issue in my submissions today, and that is the customary law status of the prohibition of terror.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. The Prosecution has made an alternative argument that, in any event, the crime of terror is reflected as part of customary international law. And our full argument on that is set our out in our response brief, paragraphs 7.27 to 6.61. We primarily rest on those submissions, and I won't repeat them before Your Honours today. But I do want to just briefly update the Chamber on one development since the brief was written, and that is the publication in 2005 of the ICRC study on customary international law which provides further support for the Prosecution's submission that the crime of terror is established in customary international law. Consistent with the approach taken by the Appeals Chamber in the Hadzihasanovic Rule 98 bis decision on 11 March 2005, the primary value of the ICRC study is the state practice and opinio juris cited rather than the formulation of the customary rules themselves by the authors of the study. In the Hadzihasanovic Rule 98 bis decision, the Appeals Chamber drew support for the customary status of the crime of wanton destruction not justified by military necessity from the state practice, namely the military manuals and national legislation, that were cited in the ICRC study. The ICRC study also sets out military manuals and national criminal codes that reflect the prohibition of terror. That's contained in volume 1, pages 9 to 10, or a summary of those, aspects of state practice is contained on those pages and set out in our supplementary book of authorities. We submit that this state practice reinforces the practice already cited in the Prosecution's response brief and reinforces the conclusion that the crime of terror is part of customary international law. The third issue in my submissions today is to explain that the crime of terror can be committed through indiscriminate attacks on civilians. Your Honours have addressed a question to the Prosecution on this issue and, in particular, you've asked us to clarify whether we believe that indiscriminate attacks can form part of the crime of terror and, if so, to provide support for our position. The short answer to this question is that the Prosecution's position is that indiscriminate attacks can form part of the crime of terror. We have expressly taken that position in our response brief at paragraphs 7.81 to 7.82 and we maintain that position. The brief also sets out a short justification for this at paragraph 7.82. We said: "The specific intent for the crime of terror will still be proved if it is established that the decision to employ indiscriminate methods was motivated by the primary objective of spreading terror." Let me assist Your Honours further with a more detailed explanation of what we mean by this and the legal reasoning and authority on which it's based. The majority convicted General Galic of the crime of terror based on what it termed "direct and indiscriminate attacks." So, for example, at paragraph 589 of the trial judgement the Chamber concluded that the majority concluded that: "The evidence ... conclusively establishes that the pattern of fire throughout the city of Sarajevo was that of indiscriminate or direct fire at civilians ... not that of fire where civilians were hit accidentally." Another similar finding is found at paragraph 591. Nonetheless, the majority still determined that the aim of the campaign was to terrorise civilians. Their approach was correct and to understand why, consider what the -- what the Trial Chamber said or meant when it said that the civilians in Sarajevo were targeted with indiscriminate fire. Of the scheduled incidents, three of the shelling cases were labelled as indiscriminate. These were numbers 1, 3 and 4. I'll start by considering incidents 3 and 4 together. Shelling incident number 3, which is found at paragraphs 331 and following of the trial judgement, was an attack in which the SRK fired three mortar shells into a residential neighbourhood of Sarajevo known as Alipasino Polje. Six children who had taken advantage of a lull in hostilities to play in the street outside their apartment buildings were killed, and other civilians, including children, were injured. Shelling incident number 4 at paragraphs 398 and following, was again an attack with three mortar shells which struck a residential neighbourhood in Dobrinja killing at least eight civilians, including a child, and injuring at least 18, including two children. During this attack, a playground that was being used by civilians for trading food and other civilian goods was hit. The methodology of the Trial Chamber in examining both of these incidents was similar. The Trial Chamber first determined that the SRK was the source of the fire. The Trial Chamber then ruled out any reasonable possibility that the fire was aimed at legitimate military objectives that may have been in the area. So, for example, the Trial Chamber noted that successive shells fired in these attacks did not fall any closer to the alleged military targets and that the shelling stopped despite the fact that no damage was in fact done to the alleged military targets. The Trial Chamber came to identically worded conclusions for each of these attacks, namely that they were: "At the very least indiscriminate as to target (which nevertheless was primarily if not entirely a residential neighbourhood) and was carried out recklessly, resulting in civilian casualties." That finding is found at paragraphs 345 and 410 of the trial judgement. What did the Chamber mean when it used the words "indiscriminate and reckless" in relation to these attacks? Well, the Trial Chamber had ruled out any possibility that the attacks were directed towards a legitimate military objective. The Trial Chamber also fell short of finding that the particular civilian victims were deliberately targeted. Against this back-drop, the characterisation of the attacks as indiscriminate as to target means that they were, at the very least, aimless attacks, in the sense that the shells were fired into residential areas without directing them at any particular targets at all. Why did the Trial Chamber describe them as reckless? Even if the civilian -- particular civilian death or injury that resulted was not the deliberate aim of the attack, they were certainly carried out knowing that it was likely civilian death and injury would result. Is there any inherent contradiction between finding that -- in finding that these indiscriminate attacks were motivated by the primary purpose of spreading terror? The answer to that question, Your Honours, must be no. Fundamentally, whether these indiscriminate attacks were carried out with the primary purpose of spreading terror is a question of fact, not of law. In this case, the evidentiary record confirms that it was the indiscriminate nature of many of the attacks in Sarajevo that reinforced the conclusion that the purpose behind the SRK's conduct was to terrify the civilian population. Why would a military force fire shells into a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, sorry for interrupting, but I -- I always control the French interpretation. There was an error in the French interpretation. It was stated that it was a matter of law and not of fact, whereas the contrary was actually stated by the speaker. I'd like to point that out now, because later on it will be too late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... note of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: I thank you my colleague from the Defence. I did indeed state it was a question of fact, not of law, and I also pointed out that it was the indiscriminate nature of the attacks in Sarajevo that underscored the Trial Chamber's -- or the majority's factual conclusion that the primary purpose was, in fact, was to spread terror. Why would -- Your Honours, why would a military force fire shells into a predominantly residential area of Sarajevo with complete abandon as to where the shells would land and with complete disregard as to whether civilians were killed or injured as a result? The reason is because it did not matter what was hit. The primary purpose of the attack was to terrify the civilian population, and in that objective, the SRK succeeded. As the majority found at paragraph 593 of the judgement, the fundamental objective of the SRK campaign was not to wipe out the civilian population but to terrify them by sending the very clear message that no Sarajevo civilian was safe anywhere at any time of day or night. Indiscriminate attacks were a particularly effective method of achieving that objective as several witnesses testified, and I've extracted fragments of their testimony as set out in the trial judgement on some slides so that Your Honour can follow while I'm proceeding. I do apologise, Your Honour, we are having some technical difficulties today. I have prepared a number of slides that we have not been able to broadcast, so I hope that the AV people may be able to assist us with fixing that problem. Okay. I understand that you can, in fact, see the slide that I prepared. I'm sorry for the interruption. So Van Lynden, a Dutch journalist, trial judgement, paragraph 575. He said that sporadic fire here and there did not serve any military goal, but the effect was to cause fear with anyone because people feared that whenever you went outside your house, you were in danger; you were never safe. Henneberry, senior UN military observer, trial judgement, paragraph 569. The shelling was designed in a manner that kept people running from building to building on their toes. Harding, UN military observer, trial judgement, paragraph 570. Shells and artillery could land virtually anywhere in the city. This way of shelling achieved maximum surprise and increased the psychological effects on the civilians of the city with a minimum of military effort. Witness Y, trial judgement, paragraph 571. The objective that the SRK forces pursued was to make every inhabitant of Sarajevo feel that nobody was sheltered or protected from the shooting and that the shooting was not aimed at military objectives but rather to increase the helplessness of the population and was aimed at cracking them and to make them collapse, nervously speaking. A similar analysis applies to the shelling incident number 1, the Dobrinja football game attack, which the Trial Chamber also regarded as an indiscriminate attack. The notion that an indiscriminate shelling campaign may amount to unlawful terrorisation of the civilian population finds support in General Assembly Resolution 53/164 on the situation of human rights in Kosevo adopted in February 1999. The General Assembly expressed grave concern about the systematic terrorisation of ethnic Albanians as demonstrated in the many reports of, among other things, indiscriminate and widespread shelling. The ICRC customary law study, volume 1, page 11, cites this resolution as an example of where indiscriminate and widespread shelling has been characterised as violating the prohibition against terror. In conclusion to my submissions on indiscriminate attacks and the crime of terror, there is no inherent inconsistency between finding that an attack which is indiscriminate in its methodology is also motivated by the primary purpose of spreading terror. The underlying objective or purpose of an attack that is indiscriminate in methodology may, in fact, be a civilian one, and the facts of this case provide a very good example of exactly that. I turn now to the fourth legal issue in my submissions today, and that is the relationship between indiscriminate, disproportionate and direct attacks, and I will respond to this issue in light of the response that the Defence has given to Your Honours question on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Ms. Jarvis, we have five minutes to go, if you can deal with your point in five minutes, I will not stop you. Otherwise, we will break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: I think I should be able to deal with it in five minutes, Your Honour, and then I will have just a very brief conclusory part to my submissions after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So then go on, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Yes. The short answer to this question is that the Trial Chamber did not characterise any of the attacks in this case as disproportionate. The Trial Chamber made a comment that the Dobrinja football game attack, even if it had been aimed at soldiers who were playing in the game, would have been disproportionate, but its operative finding was that the SRK did not know that the soldiers were there and that the attack consequently could not have been aimed at these soldiers. It held that the attack was indiscriminate. As to the attacks characterised as indiscriminate, the Chamber when applying the facts to the law, used the label "indiscriminate" and did not refer to them as direct attacks. And I've already referred Your Honours to the findings at paragraph 589 and 591. There is no reversible error in this respect. The Appeals Chamber's question does raise, though, the more theoretical issue of the relationship between the various terms that are used for unlawful attacks, direct attacks, making civilians the object of attack, indiscriminate attacks and disproportionate attacks. This is particularly so in light of the Trial Chamber's finding at paragraphs 57 and 60 of the judgement, where, in setting out the applicable law, the Chamber recognised that indiscriminate and disproportionate attacks may qualify as direct attacks. The Prosecution's submission is that the Trial Chamber was right in this part of its legal analysis. Indiscriminate and disproportionate attacks can be equated with making civilians the object of attack or direct attacks. Direct attacks include all attacks that violate the principle of distinction, because either the target selected is not limited to a military objective or because the attack is carried out using a methodology that is incapable of distinguishing between military objectives and civilians to the extent required by the principle of proportionality. Consider, Your Honours, the following examples. The deliberate sniping of a civilian on the streets of Sarajevo. This is an attack in which the target selected is civilian and, as a result, it violates the principle of distinction and constitutes a direct attack on a civilian. The second example, lobbing shells randomly into the city of Sarajevo without regard as to what target is hit. As I've previously explained, this kind of attack is indiscriminate in the sense that the methodology of the attack is incapable of drawing a distinction between military and civilian objectives as required, for example, by Article 51(4) of Protocol I dealing with indiscriminate attacks. It violates the principle that only legitimate military objectives can be selected as the target of an attack and it is properly regarded as a direct attack. It would have been open to the Trial Chamber in this case to use that label when it applied the facts of this case to the law. My third example is where a party to a conflict might select a legitimate military target in conformity with the principle of distinction but aim to neutralise it using a methodology that cannot distinguish between military and civilian targets as required by the principle of proportionality. So, for example, dropping a bomb on a village in order to target a soldier who is home on leave. This attack is indiscriminate in methodology. In particular, it violates the principle of proportionality and, because of that, the principle of distinction. Proceeding with such an attack, in knowledge that civilian casualties will be excessive in relation to the direct and concrete military objective accrued, can properly be regarded in substance as an attack that is directed against civilians. Incidental civilian damage ceases to be incidental, or secondary, if you like, if the rule of proportionality is breached. This approach finds support in several sources. For example, the ICRC study on customary international law, volume 1, at page 601, states that: "Both indiscriminate and disproportionate attacks can be likened to attacks on civilians if the perpetrator was aware that this would be the effect of the attack in the ordinary course of events." I also refer Your Honours to the decision in the International Court of Justice in the Nuclear Weapons Advisory Opinion, paragraph 78, which is also cited in the trial judgement at footnote 101. With regard to the obligation of states not to make civilians the object of attack, the ICJ stated that: "They must consequently never use weapons that are incapable of distinguishing between military and civilian targets. Similar reasoning was set out by Judge Higgins in her dissenting opinion in that case at paragraph 22, and these references are all in our supplementary book of authorities. Similarly, Louise Doswald-Beck, in her 1997 article on the ICJ Advisory Opinion, in our book of authorities, concludes from the ICJ's reasoning that: "The prohibition against deliberately attacking civilians found in Article 13 of Additional Protocol II (which is in identical terms to Article 51(2) of Protocol I) automatically means that indiscriminate weapons must not be used in non-international armed conflicts." Article 13 of Protocol II includes only the prohibition on making civilians the object of attack. It does not include the express references to indiscriminate or disproportionate attacks. Consistent with the view expressed by Louise Doswald-Beck, the ICRC commentary to Article 13 of Protocol II at paragraph 4764 states that this nevertheless does not reduce the degree of protection accorded to civilians in internal armed conflicts. I also refer Your Honours to Bothe and Partsch who take a similar position, and that's contained in our supplementary book of authorities. In conclusion to my submissions on this issue, the Trial Chamber did not, when it applied the facts to the law in this case, equate indiscriminate attacks on civilians with direct attacks, but it would have been open to the Trial Chamber to do so, as indeed the Chamber had recognised earlier in its legal discussion in the judgement. If it is convenient, Your Honours, I'll rest my submissions there for the moment and finish when we return from the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. We will break now and we will reconvene at 2.15 p.m. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.33 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. We resume the hearing on this appeal. I will give the floor to the Prosecution to continue their response. They have 45 minutes from now to conclude their response. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Well, Your Honours will be pleased to hear that I have reached the fifth and final issue that I wanted to address before you today, and that is that there was no error in the Trial Chamber clarifying the elements of torture and in this respect modifying them from those proposed by the Prosecution at trial. Full submissions on this issue are set out in our response brief, but to further assist in explaining why this complaint that the Defence have raised is without foundation, I have prepared a chart which compares the crime of terror, the elements proposed by the Prosecution with those found by the Chamber, and I'll ask that that be put up on the screen now for Your Honours to view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: We have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. You can see from this chart, Your Honours, that in fact the elements proposed by the Prosecution and those found by the Chamber are substantially similar. The main difference stems from the fact that whereas the Prosecution submitted elements for the crime of terror based on the full breadth of the crime of terror, and by that I mean both acts and threats of violence, the Chamber found that it only had to pronounce on a more limited situation where acts of violence have resulted in civilian death and injury, which is what arose on the facts of this case. So with respect to element 1 set out in the chart, the Prosecution submitted acts or threats of violence, the Trial Chamber limited its consideration to acts of violence. Element 2 is the result requirement for unlawful attacks. This stems from Article 85 of Protocol I which mandates that to be a criminal offence, the unlawful attack must result in death or serious injury to body or health. When it came to the limited subset of the crime of terror before it, the Chamber found that the result requirement was satisfied by proof of civilian death or injury and that it was not necessary to look separately at whether terror was actually inflicted. There is no valid complaint about the Trial Chamber's conclusion that in cases where the result requirement for criminalisation is met through proof of civilian death or injury, it was not necessary to look separately at whether there was also actual infliction of terror. Most importantly, the essence of the crime of terror and what justifies the application of the separate label of terror over and above other types of unlawful attacks is the specific intent requirement, the primary purpose of spreading terror, and in this the elements proposed by the Prosecution and accepted by the Chamber are identical. To conclude my submissions, when General Galic commanded his SRK forces in Sarajevo, he could not have genuinely believed that attacking civilians, causing death and injury in order to terrify them and force a capitulation of the enemy was a legitimate tactic of war that could not be subject to criminal sanction. States have long condemned this sort of terrorisation, and the parties to the conflict in Bosnia had specifically agreed that it was impermissible and subject to criminal sanction. What is quite believable, though, is that General Galic, carrying out this campaign of terror, thought that he would never be prosecuted for this offence, that he would enjoy the same impunity that has undermined the implementation of humanitarian law for so long. The very reason for this Tribunal's establishment was to change all of that. The Trial Chamber was right to label this psychological warfare against the civilians of Sarajevo as the crime of terror and to hold General Galic accountable for the role that he played in it. That concludes my submissions, Your Honour, and unless there are any questions that you would like me to address at this point, I'll hand the podium over to my colleague, Mr. Ierace, who is going to address you in relation to the principles of distinction and proportionality and the Trial Chamber's conclusions on that and its evaluation of the evidence. He'll also answer Your Honours' question as to return fire on the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. May I turn to my colleagues if they want to take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE FRENCH INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Ms. Jarvis, before the break you tried to make the equivalent between indiscriminate and disproportionate attacks on the one hand with direct attacks on civilians on the other hand. My question to you is this: To establish the crime of terror, do we need to equate indiscriminate or disproportionate attacks with direct attacks against civilians? This is my question to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer to that question is no. It is not necessary to establish the crime of terror to equate them. We say that the equation of the two is correct, as a matter of law, but even if Your Honours were to be against us on that point, that would not preclude a finding on the facts of this case that indiscriminate attacks, however qualified, could form part of the crime of terror.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. One short and one slightly longer question. First of all, you mentioned a series of attacks directed on civilians. Where is the threshold and what is the distinguishing element, because it seems to be hardly conceivable to carry out such a series of direct attacks on civilians without the purpose to spread terror. Secondly, the more serious question is: What about the penalisation? In Article 50 (1), (2), it only reads that these acts are prohibited. And in a long chapter in the judgement there are references made to an agreement; I think it was 22nd of May. Do you think at all that it is necessary to refer to this agreement? You made the argument that first treaty law is applicable, also customary international law foresees the penalisation of such a conduct, but isn't it true that also the law of former Yugoslavia already foresaw, as it is stated in the judgement itself, that such -- the purpose to spread terror amongst civilians is already penalised in Yugoslavia, and this is a clear indication that Yugoslavia, having ratified the Geneva Protocols, including the first Additional Protocol, that they have implemented, as such, the Geneva Conventions, and therefore this agreement often quoted in the judgement is nothing but a declaration of the awareness of these -- of the participants having signed this document, that it is penalised in the area in former Yugoslavia and then that they are bound by this penalisation? And you mentioned, to conclude the question, the subject matter, jurisdiction in the report of Security Council in the beginning, also referring to domestic law in para 36, and isn't it true that this entire chapter doesn't create any kind of hierarchy between treaty law, customary international law, domestic law, but that what is even underlined in paragraph 34, that the rationale of this -- these paragraphs is that there is no crime without law? So, in conclusion, how is your approach to go one step further, that it's not only prohibited but that it's penalised?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will respond to the second question first, if I may, and then I apologise but I may need to seek a clarification of the first question, because I'm not sure that I understood entirely what it is that Your Honour would most like me to address, so I will ask for clarification of that. But as to your second question which, as I understand it, relates to how do we make our way through this maze of convention, special agreement, customary law on the point of the criminalisation of the crime of terror in particular, Your Honour, we submit that the way the Trial Chamber approached this matter was correct. They looked first and foremost at the 22nd of May agreement, which was a special agreement entered into by the parties to the conflict in Bosnia as envisaged by common Article 3 to the Geneva Conventions. The reason why it is important to look at the effect of that document is because the parties agreed to apply the provisions of Protocol I of the Geneva Conventions, regardless of the classification of the conflict. So by virtue of the 22 May agreement, the parties made it clear that they were going to comply with the rules applicable to international armed conflicts, regardless of the status of the conflict in Bosnia. So that was what justified the Trial Chamber's conclusion that it wasn't necessary to characterise the conflict in this case because the applicable norms are the same regardless. In terms of the validity of domestic law and the way that that fits into this equation, the Appeals Chamber has of course noted that it does not have jurisdiction over domestic law per se. That's not to say that domestic law is irrelevant, as I think it was the Appeals Chamber in the Ojdanic joint criminal enterprise appeal decision stated that domestic law, even if not an independent source of law, is nevertheless of assistance in assessing the compliance with the principle of nullum crimen because it may serve to make a particular prohibition accessible to an accused person. So we say it is relevant in that regard. And it is also relevant, as Your Honour rightly points out, because the 22nd May agreement specifically applying Article 51 of Protocol I stated in one of its later clauses in the document, that breaches set out in the 22nd of May agreement would be punished in accordance with domestic law and therefore, Your Honour, it quite correctly points out that there was a history of legislation in the former Yugoslavia which implemented that country's obligations under Protocol I to provide a domestic forum for the Prosecution of these offences. In terms of customary law, we say the Trial Chamber was correct to conclude it didn't have to go into that question because the 22 May agreement was sufficient in terms of demonstrating both the prohibition and the criminalisation. But even if Your Honours were against us on that, we say that the prohibition on terror is established as part of customary international law, and we've set out detailed submissions on that in our brief as supplemented in my submissions today. Unless Your Honours have any particular aspects of that that you would like me to address in more detail, I'll rest on what we've said in the brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just to clarify, is it your proposition that this agreement constitutes new law or the penalisation, or is it more or less a declaration of already-existing law accepted by the parties, again, therefore having no constitutive force at all. And to repeat the minor question immediately that I don't take the floor again, my question was only what is the distinguishing element between attacks against civilians and whether it's conceivable at all to carry out such a series of attacks directed on civilians without the purpose to spread terror, referring to, in particular, those expert witness testimonies you showed us this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in respect of your follow-up question to the answer I've just given you, I would just say that the effect of the 22nd of May, 1992, agreement was not to constitute new law. That can't be the case because of course it was already provided for in the domestic system of Yugoslavia. But what that agreement did was take the relevant domestic law and make it applicable as part of a special agreement as provided for in common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions and by virtue of that take it out of purely the realm of domestic law and into the realm of an international agreement over which this Tribunal has jurisdiction. In respect of the other point that you raised, thank you for the clarification, I do understand now, certain -- I suppose Your Honour's question raises two points primarily. First of all, obviously, it is generally going to be the case that any unlawful attack or even any lawful attack against civilians will in fact result in terror. And it's clear that when the drafters of Protocol I, Article 51, were intending to prohibit this particular type of offence, that's not the kind of terror they had in mind, and that's why they included the special intent requirement that the primary purpose of the acts of violence or the threats of violence must be to spread terror. And we say there is no problem with that on the facts of this case because, as I started my submission saying, this wasn't just the inevitable terror that accompanies conflict, terror that accompanies conflict. As the majority went to lengths to point out in their reasoning, this was a calculated, modulated campaign specifically designed to inflict terror. But the second point that Your Honour's question raises is whether it is ever possible to have a series of attacks like this directed at civilians without meeting the specific intent requirement. Your Honours, theoretically that might be the case. For example, it might be the primary purpose to in fact not spread terror but to wipe out the population, to completely annihilate them through death and injury. In that case, the specific intent, the primary purpose, would not be to spread terror but to kill them. But that was expressly not the finding of the majority in this case. They said it wasn't a campaign designed to annihilate the population and it was a campaign, the primary purpose of which was to spread terror.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for both clarifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Here is a little one I'm sure you will knock down with a feather. It is, however, troubling me and so I put it to you for your help. Suppose two other warring parties in the former Yugoslavia had entered into an agreement conferring jurisdiction on the Tribunal over terror, but had accompanied that prescription by certain other provisions which were not on par with the normal provision. Suppose, for example, they had said that, all right, the Tribunal will have jurisdiction over terror, provided, however, that the maximum sentence should not be beyond, say, ten years. Well, then, I gather from your presentation that the Tribunal would be in the unhappy position of having to execute both agreements, differing as to sentences, but agreeing as to the crime. Help me out on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll respond by making two main points in relation to that question. And the first point is that the point of this Tribunal's jurisdiction extending to clearly applicable treaty provisions is of course to address the problem of nullum crimen sine lege, to ensure that this Tribunal doesn't retrospectively penalise acts, activities that were not penalisable or were not criminal at the time that they were committed. This Tribunal has never been confined in its sentencing practice by domestic legislation or any other provision in international law. So we would submit that while it would be appropriate to look at that agreement and be satisfied that nullum crimen concerns had been met, that that would not limit this Tribunal's sentencing jurisdiction in the normal course. And I perhaps could also, as my second point, point Your Honours to the Kordic appeal judgement where perhaps a somewhat similar situation arose in the way the Chamber approached the question. Because there the Chamber was looking at the issue of the result requirement for criminalisation of unlawful attacks, and it was applying the provisions of Protocol I as a matter of treaty law. And the Chamber looked at Article 85 and determined that, indeed, the result requirement of serious death and injury was mandatory. But the Appeals Chamber went on to look at whether there was a different position in customary international law, whether there was any evidence that this result requirement had in fact been modified by a customary law norm, and it would seem from that approach that the Chamber was open to the idea that even if there is a clearly applicable treaty provision, if there was a broader customary law norm the Tribunal would in fact go with that approach, and we say that is also a response to Your Honour's question on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I have heard you. Can you help me on a related question? I gather your position is this: That even if the Tribunal has no jurisdiction over treaty-based crimes, where the treaty has not evolved into customary international law, the crime in question was still known to customary international law, is that your position and, if so, could you help me again by telling me what is your strongest argument for saying that terror was known to customary international law at the material times?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: If Your Honour would just allow me one moment to reflect on the answer that I would wish to give to that question. Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, I can clarify that it is the Prosecution's position that in any event the crime of terror is reflected in customary international law. As you would have seen from our brief, we have approached that question from a number of different angles, as indeed the Trial Chamber did, and we say that's correct. But if I was to put to Your Honours the strongest of our arguments in that respect, I would say that there is sufficient state practice and opinio juris as cited in our brief and supplemented by the ICRC study on customary international law to establish this norm as a matter of customary law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other questions? If that's not the case, please, the Prosecution can continue their submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The main focus of my submissions this afternoon is a response to the written submissions of the Defence but I will incorporate into that a response to some of the submissions that have been made this morning. I might indicate for the benefit of the interpreters that I understand a copy of my response is being prepared for them, to assist them. Your Honours, in his written submissions, the appellant contended that the Trial Chamber approached the evaluation of the evidence in an erroneous fashion. I'm referring to grounds 11, 12, 14, 15 and 17. A predominant theme in these grounds is that no, or insufficient attention was paid by the majority, and Judge Nieto-Navia, in his separate judgement, to the principles of distinction and proportionality and, in particular, to evidence that the city was replete with military targets. Accordingly, says the appellant, what appeared to the witnesses called by the Prosecution to have been attacks on civilians could have been, in fact, proportionate attacks directed to military targets. Around this central theme, the appellant has appended secondary arguments. For example, that the evidence of the totality of civilian casualties in Sarajevo in the indictment period is inconsistent with deliberate attacks on citizens and consistent instead with attacks against military targets that proportionately incurred civilian casualties, an argument adopted by Judge Nieto-Navia and repeated this morning by Mr. Piletta-Zanin. I will come to it. The appellant argues that the Trial Chamber failed to consider this possibility that civilian casualties were an unavoidable corollary of these lawful attacks; for example, in ground 11, paragraph 127, that the Prosecution had to prove that civilian casualties were not the result of collateral damage. Ground 12 is concerned with the same issue. Ground 14 as well, in so far as it deals with the alleged failure of the Trial Chamber to define civilian and military areas. In ground 15, the Defence argues it was necessary for the SRK to use mortars in order to take out military targets obstructed from their view and again, accordingly, civilian deaths were an unavoidable consequence of a legitimate military action. A second theme also emerges from these grounds, in relation to the alleged --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Excuse me, I see the Defence. You have a --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. If you make quotations or references, it should be done normally, in the Defence's view, from the transcript. I can see that we never indicated that we would argue that the result of these casualties were the acceptable result of unlawful attacks. We said the contrary. I just wanted to clarify this because when I work on the French transcript I want everything to be clear. Thank you very much, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. A second theme also emerges from these same grounds in relation to the alleged erroneous approach of the Trial Chamber to the evaluation of evidence. The appellant has submitted that the Trial Chamber moved from "the general to the particular." It concluded there was a campaign of targeting civilians based on a generalised overview evidence of the sniping and shelling in the city and separately made findings that particular scheduled incidents were proved. So says the appellant. These submissions are in the appellant's ground 12 at paragraphs 117 to 119 and ground 17 at paragraph 255. The appellant contends that the scheduled incidents were insufficient to prove a widespread and systematic campaign but the overview evidence did not involve evidence of provable specific incidents, were not based on knowledge of the whereabouts of military targets and therefore was unreliable. The Prosecution submits that both of these attacks on the judgements are without merit. The Trial Chamber noted the particularisation of specific incidents in the indictment was a procedural requirement of the Tribunal's jurisprudence that gave the appellant proper notice of the case he had to meet, paragraph 188 of the judgement, but by complying with that procedure, the Prosecution did not limit its case to them. Even in relation to the unscheduled incidents, particulars, some particulars were provided by the Prosecution to the Defence as part of its Rule 65 ter obligations. The majority understood that these scheduled incidents were not intended to represent, nor were they capable of representing, a widespread and systematic campaign, and for that reason, the Trial Chamber had regard to the evidence led -- I should say the majority had regard to the evidence led by the Prosecution to prove that these incidents were not isolated but representative of a campaign, paragraph 208.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will. The Trial Chamber said that to the extent that was possible and reasonable, it assessed each scheduled incident on its own terms but also with a limited reference to other evidence concerning the situation of civilians in Sarajevo, paragraph 207. These pockets of scheduled incident-specific evidence were then considered by the Trial Chamber: "Within a more general evidentiary context reflecting how the great number of witnesses in the case understood them and explained them." Paragraph 189. Accordingly, it is not correct to suggest that the Trial Chamber considered the overview evidence and the evidence pertaining to the scheduled incidents separately. Ultimately, it combined all the evidence, including that of the unscheduled incidents, in a global fashion as it was entitled to do and as common sense would dictate. The Trial Chamber also considered the evidence from different perspectives, from the geographical perspective and the temporal perspective. It weighed the evidence district by district around Sarajevo as to scheduled and unscheduled sniping and shelling incidents and the evidence of the whereabouts of possible military targets, in great detail, accounting for 150 pages of the judgement. The Trial Chamber explained that in this exhaustive review: "Witness evidence, together with documentary evidence, has been chosen, combined and arranged by the Trial Chamber in accordance with its relevance the credibility of its source, and its probative value, with due regard to the fact that the present indictment alleges unlawful conduct and responsibility for such conduct going beyond what is referred to in the scheduled incidents." Paragraph 189. The Trial Chamber repeatedly considered possible exculpatory evidence consistent with the principles of distinction and proportionality but outlined its approach to this evidence at paragraphs 185 to 191, stating that it had regard to: "Combat activity going on at the time and the location of the incident as well as relevant nearby presence of military activities and facilities." The majority concluded that throughout the indictment period, wherever there were civilians within the confrontation lines, this is as a result of their district by district consideration of the evidence, considering the scheduled incidents, the unscheduled incidents and the overview incidents, that civilians were targeted often from places that gained local notoriety such as the Grbavica high-rise buildings on the sniper alley, General Tito Boulevard, Ozrenska Street onto Hrasno, the church tower on to Dobrinja, the ridge known as "sharp stone" into north eastern Sarajevo, and so on. This targeting was overwhelmingly from SRK forces and in an orchestrated manner that was demonstrated to be responsive to the SRK leadership. The Trial Chamber also considered the overall pattern of fire throughout the indictment period, noting the fluctuations and diminution in civilian casualties as civilians individually, the Sarajevan civil authorities and the UN devised successful protective strategies. Civilians were forced from the relative safety of their homes to fetch water, to find combustible material to burn for cooking and warmth. As time passed, safer alternative pedestrian routes to traverse the city were developed, funerals were held at night, pedestrian crossings were afforded some protection with shipping containers and the like, the cover of foggy mornings was used to cross open ground, and so the rate of civilian casualties dropped over the period. The appellant submitted to the Trial Chamber in going beyond the evidence pertaining to the scheduled incidents, relied on a body of witnesses whose credibility was unreliable. "These testimonies do not contain even a single concrete data on the alleged incidents." Paragraph 255, grounds 17. And we heard that again today from Mrs. Pilipovic. The Prosecution submits this submission is contrary to the trial record. The evidence before the Trial Chamber included that of insiders who gave evidence of SRK practice in relation to the shelling of civilians deliberately, and the indiscriminate targeting of civilians through sniping. In relation to shelling, to use the words of the majority, Witness AD, a SRK soldier, testified that the commander of the Ilijas Brigade, and that was one of the brigades of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps gave orders to his mortar battery to target ambulances, a marketplace, funeral processions, and cemeteries further north from the city in Mrakovo. In relation to sniping, Witness D, also an SRK soldier, gave evidence of serving with snipers both at the Grbavica high-rise buildings overlooking central Sarajevo and also at SRK positions just north of Ozrenska Street on the ridge to the south of the city overlooking Hrasno. He described their sniper rifles, fitted with telescopic sights. At Grbavica they were ordered to shoot anything that moved. They were not ordered to not target civilians. Paragraphs 236, 237 of the judgement indicates that Their Honours accepted this evidence. At Ozrenska Street, Witness D saw infrared sights and a special machine-gun fitted with an optical sight. From that position, he saw the gunners targeting intersections that, although protected with anti-sniping barriers, still allowed opportunities to snipe people visible in gaps between the barriers. Mrs. Pilipovic said even yet again this morning that there was no evidence that the SRK had snipers, in spite of the uncontradicted evidence of Witness D. It was not put to him that he was lying or mistaken. Even the Defence's own command and control expert, General Radinovic, in his report tendered by the Defence said that the SRK had snipers from 1993. As well as the insiders, the Trial Chamber heard from war correspondents, seasoned observers of armed conflict. Aernout Van Lynden, an ex-member of the Royal Netherlands Marine Corps, toured the entire front line with the permission of General Mladic, accompanied by liaison officers of the SRK, and he personally inspected the sniper outposts in the Grbavica high-rise. He noted the snipers wore uniforms, that they used radios and spotters to conduct their sniping from those positions. He gave evidence that on the 5th of December, 1992, he observed a civilian apartment block come under fire. On that day, he saw the shelling of the apartment block in Cengic Vila, that particular part of Sarajevo, he marked the position of the apartment block with precision on a map. He saw it come under fire from incendiary rounds of a large calibre, he estimated 10 to 15 centimetres, either a very large machine-gun or anti-aircraft gun. Because they were incendiary, he could easily visually trace them back to their source on SRK territory. He knew it was that because he had been there. His film crew took some footage in his presence, Exhibit P3647, which we will see now, part of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: "One apartment block, the resident watching, distraught, his home, belongings gone. "Seconds later, further bursts of incendiary rounds crash into the building or bounce off the wall into the street below. Wanton arson of a purely civilian target. "As ever, Sarajevo's remarkable firemen fight back, getting their hoses to the flames for once unhampered by a cut in the water supply. But for the fire chief water is not the main concern. His engines are running out of fuel. And he tells us he won't be able to cope with another fire this day. "The fall of artillery and escalation of shelling here in the centre of Sarajevo again undermine the impotence of international efforts in Bosnia. Cease-fires and political talks have led no where and won't until the western world proves it has a true commitment in ending this war. Aernout Van Lynden, SkyNews, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Van Lynden gave evidence that he personally interviewed some of the hundreds of civilians who lived in the building, and they confirmed there was no military occupation of any part of the building, that fire did not emanate from it, and that the fire against them commenced without warning with the incendiary rounds. Your Honours, I'm aware I only have five minutes left, so I will move in more or less point form through some of the rest of what I wish to submit. Another witness, equally impressive, was Morten Hvaal, a Norwegian photojournalist with 20 years experience. He gave evidence of convincing unscheduled incidents; for example, whilst driving along General Tito Boulevard in the winter of either 1993 or 1994, he observed a middle-aged woman who had been shot in the lower portion of her body writhing in an intersection which was exposed to fire from SRK territory to the south. He observed pedestrians from a position of cover attempting to rescue her. He tried to use his armoured journalist's vehicle to protect her from the south, but before he could take those measures she was shot in the head. He then accompanied the transport of her body to the morgue, where he photographed it, and that's in evidence. P3625. It is convincing visual evidence that she was shot as a civilian, being elderly, wearing a fur coat, makeup, having long hair. The Tribunal -- the Trial Chamber heard from 21 UN military personnel who witnessed the conflict on the ground during the appellant's tenure. They had an office in his headquarters. They explained the relatively static nature of the conflict, the fact that there was little movement on the lines accepted by the majority at paragraph 589. That is a very important aspect of understanding the evidence, Your Honours, in this case. It was an unusual armed conflict because over the extended period of the indictment, there was very little movement in terms of the front line. There were occasional flare-ups but even those had mostly subsided by the end of 1992. They gave evidence of observing multi-launch rocket systems impacting in the city. Carl Harding, on the 8th of December, 1992, saw nine rockets hit the downtown part of Sarajevo. Major Jeremy Hermer, likewise in October 1993. These are what are called, according to the experts in the trial, area weapons, anti-personnel weapons, designed to create a large killing field area of shrapnel, not designed to demolish buildings as was the case with mortars. Mr. Piletta-Zanin this morning referred to most of the damage being on the front lines. That may have been the case. There was evidence that there was significant damage downtown as well, but the weapons that were aimed at the civilians were anti-personnel weapons rather than those designed to damage buildings. The fact that Their Honours occasionally rejected scheduled incidents demonstrated the care that they employed in considering the principle of proportionality and an honest and understandable mistake on the part of the SRK. An example of that is sniping incident 14. Although the Trial Chamber concluded the victim was an unarmed civilian wearing civilian clothes engaged in a civilian activity, having regard to his proximity to a military check-point and that he was advancing towards the front line when he was shot and poor visibility, it said: "That it could not exclude" -- "cannot exclude beyond reasonable doubt that Witness L was deliberately targeted as a civilian and cannot consider this incident as representative of a campaign of fire against civilians." Your Honours, in the remaining few minutes, I would respectfully submit that Your Honours look at the 360-degree photographs which are in evidence; for example, in relation to sniping incident 6. One will come on the screen in a moment. They demonstrate how, while it would have been preferable for the Trial Chamber to have a view, it was not absolutely necessary. Ms. Pilipovic said this morning that with a view the Trial Chamber could have seen if there was a line of sight from where the victim was to where the suspected source of fire was. They had that advantage with these 360-degree photographs. The modus was that an video would be tendered into evidence. On the video, the Trial Chamber could see an eye-witness to the sniping incident, indicate with position -- precision, rather, where the victim was when shot, the eye-witness would confirm that in live evidence before the Tribunal. There was evidence that the camera would then be set up on a special tripod at precisely that position at the approximate height at which the bullet entered the body, and then 360 photographs such as this generated. Incident 6 involved a middle-aged woman who was shot while collecting water from the banks of the Dobrinja river. She and others had been sheltering from sniper fire beside a pedestrian bridge. And as we turn the photograph around, we can see the river and the overhead bridge, and in the distance, the witness -- the eye-witness was able to identify a particular building which was a suspected source of fire. It's possible to zoom in on these photographs, and I won't take Your Honours to them now because of lack of time. But Your Honours will see by looking at the evidence in relation to this incident that the still photograph was generated of the view on the screen at the moment, the particular building was circled, further photographs were tendered of that building, including an area map, and that was ultimately appropriately identified. Your Honours have asked a question in relation to returned fire to hospitals. Perhaps I should deal with that very quickly. The wording of the question by the use of the word "may" appropriately incorporates a qualification for the hospital does not necessarily lose its protection simply because troops have fired from it. The effect of Additional Protocol -- it's well established that hospitals are protected, and the effect of Additional Protocol I, Articles 8 and 12, is that they are protected at all times and should not be the object of attack. Such an attack constitutes a grave breach of Additional Protocol I. The Additional Protocols provide that due warning must be given by the retaliatory party with reasonable notice to evacuate. That notice must be long enough, according to the ICRC commentary either to allow the unlawful acts to be stopped or for wounded -- the wounded and sick who are present to be removed to a place of safety. The special agreement of the 22nd of May, 1992, on the application of international humanitarian law between the parties at paragraph 2.2 specified that where hospitals were used to commit military acts, they would lose their protection only "after due warning and a reasonable time limit to cease military activities." As to when an attack should cease, given that it could only proceed in the first place in conformity with the principles of distinction and proportionality, those same principles must surely guide the time at which it must cease. In other words, a hospital that loses its protection from attack ceases to be a legitimate military target and regains that protection when the attack no longer complies with those two principles. To apply that to the situation established in the evidence in relation to Kosevo hospital, which I assume was the motivation, the SRK should have ceased its counter-battery fire when the mortars and the crew could no longer be expected to be present, or when the anticipated civilian casualties and damage to the hospital was excessive in contrast to the remaining expectations of neutralising the mortar unit or units by further fire. Excuse me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, may I draw your attention to the clock. Your time has expired.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Unless Your Honours have any questions, I'll cease my submissions at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions from the Bench? Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I have noticed that you have not really discussed in detail the Markale market situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Indeed I had intended to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could I ask you then a question which might help you focus on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I have two questions with regard to that. You will recall the UNPROFOR report which is cited in the judgement. That report states, and I quote: "That it was not possible to estimate with any acceptable degree of accuracy the angle of descent of the shell that hit Markale market and that UNPROFOR therefore could only conclude that the possible distance of origin of fire is between 300 metres and 5.551 metres." In these circumstances, on what basis could a reasonable Trial Chamber conclude that the angle of descent was no greater than 65 degrees and that the shot therefore came from behind Serb lines? This is my first question. I will have one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are perhaps two bodies of evidence that were of great assistance to the Trial Chamber in arriving at that conclusion beyond a reasonable doubt. The first was the supplementary, what we might call the supplementary expert evidence available to the Trial Chamber which was not available to the UN at that particular point in time in 1994. In particular, I refer to the evidence of Mr. Zecevic, the Prosecution expert, and the investigations that he carried out. There was also some other material beyond him that went into evidence that supplemented the material before the UN. Secondly, the second fundamental body of evidence was that of what might be loosely called eye-witnesses, perhaps ear witnesses. There were three civilians who were positioned at the relevant time in close proximity to the confrontation line in the relevant part of Sarajevo. Mr. Piletta-Zanin referred to one of them, AK-1, this morning. That witness was not the only source of such evidence. I especially refer Your Honours to I think it was Witness P, who was positioned some 200 metres beneath sharp stone at the appropriate time, and Witness P gave evidence of hearing an explosion consistent with the firing of a heavy weapon coming from beyond the reach, and given that the SRK occupied the ridge, beyond the ridge clearly meant in SRK territory. And shortly after, that witness made observations consistent with the shell having exploded in Markale. So there was -- those -- the evidence of those three witnesses to supplement not only the UN report but the additional expert evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. My second question is this: Let us assume, indeed, that the shell which hit Markale market was fired by Serb forces. Given that according to Witness Hamill, who was cited by the Prosecution this morning, the closest legitimate military target was just 300 metres away. On what basis could a reasonable Trial Chamber conclude that the shell was fired deliberately at the market?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The evidence that that was so, that the Trial Chamber could have regard to, was the considerable body of evidence that because of the unusual feature of this armed conflict that I referred to earlier, namely its static nature, mortar crews were able in this particular conflict to achieve an extraordinary degree of accuracy with their firing. Even Witness AD, who was the captain of a mortar crew, testified that he was capable of hitting a moving target. Mr. Ashton, a humanitarian supplier of medical supplies, witnessed such an attack on a vehicle. As the vehicle drove down the road, it was being followed by mortars until finally hit. That is a degree of accuracy which normally is not capable of being achieved. The specific reason that they could do that was because as explained by the mortar experts, a mortar has what's called a ground plate underneath it, and when that is firmly anchored, such accuracy is capable, together with the knowledge of coordinates that are used time and time again. These mortars on the SRK side did not have to be moved. Because of the imbalance in heavy weaponry between the two sides, the SRK did not fear that their mortar sites would be attacked by the ABiH, so they remained in position for two years and therefore were very accurate. However, it was not the Prosecution case that the market was definitely specifically targeted. Rather, that equally it could have been a case of indiscriminate fire, given that it was one shell fired into that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So the Prosecution does not, in fact, argue that this was deliberate?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The Prosecution, in a sense, has it both ways, Your Honour, that the accuracy of the crews was such that it could have been deliberately targeted, but in any event, it was indiscriminate to send a shell into that area. Your Honour mentioned that there was evidence of a military target some 300 metres away. The Prosecution would strongly submit that that could not excuse the firing of a 120-millimetre mortar shell, which is a very big mortar shell, into the crowded downtown area of Sarajevo around mid-day on a Friday. I indicate that day because it was well known that that was a market day, a green market day, and a number of casualties from one single shell in the hundreds, attests to that, how tightly packed civilians were at that stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I seem to remember that there was some testimony to the effect that an experienced mortar crew would on the first shell be able to get within 200, 300 metres. We are talking this is in the same ballpark and there was only one shell fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. And what Your Honour says firstly is an accurate rendition of the evidence, and it's what properly applies to what we might call a normal armed conflict but not to a static conflict as there was in Sarajevo. And again, I would refer Your Honour to extensive evidence to the effect that this unusual feature, both in the Prosecution final submissions, post-trial, as well as the oral submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I turn now to the Defence for their reply. The Defence has scheduled 45 minutes for their reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So we have 45 minutes, right? We have 45 minutes, Mr. President? Yes. Very well. Thank you very much, Mr. President. I am going to respond a little more slowly so as to avoid any translation problems. Let me start with what Mr. Ierace said in his responses and then I'll go back to the other features that may be necessary. First point, it is being told to you that this weapon, and it is now discovered that this shell on Markale may not have been a deliberate attack but a reckless act. It is also being told to you that the Serbs were very accurate in their firing. But one thing is not mentioned and has been neglected, whilst it has been proved each mortar shell, each mortar fire must be looked as an individual case because at the weather conditions on a day are never the same as on the next day or the day before. So everything is in flux and changes. So theoretically on a range of 5.000 or 6.000 metres, if you have a few more or less degrees in temperature or more wind or less wind, that will change the target, not by 200 but by 500 or 600 metres. An expert said so. The mortar weapon is an area weapon, so you can of course hit -- you say you can move -- hit a moving vehicle, well, good luck to you if you try. That will be my first point. Secondly, if I do follow the Prosecution, it is impossible to fire with heavy weaponry in a town on objects such as barracks. If I did understand the Prosecution well, any fire on civilians is terror. So there is no need to make any distinction they say. They say in theory, it is sufficient for the wish to eliminate a population in Sarajevo or elsewhere, then the problem of terror is eliminated too. It's a little easy. It is all theory. But let's look at the concrete situation for this man who is being tried and not for another, for Mr. Mladic or somebody else. You must see whether in Sarajevo 120-millimetre mortar shells did occasion impermissible damage. And the graph does show that there were 120-, 80-, 60-millimetre shells but there was a will on behalf of the command to comply with the two main principles of distinction and proportionality, and that is what happened in the figures. Thank you for admitting for the first time today, Mr. Ierace, that possibly there was not that degree of destruction within the centre of Sarajevo. You just admit the truth, nothing more, nothing less. You admit that damage was mainly caused on the confrontation line, and this changes the whole ball game, but it's only admitted now. Now as to the other answers to be supplied, some are important ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask you to slow down or slow down again?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll slow down again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Think of the interpreters, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies to everybody. So terror and fire directed at the population. I'd like to say one thing once again. The Serb forces, they didn't have a plan. A plan was never seen, the goals of the superiors as they say. They were never seen. We don't know what they are. How can you carry out something that could not be proved at trial? But they were indeed objectives. There were two of them. They were material military objectives. This or that object, a table, or this or that object, and there were also strategic objectives. You know the military. As to strategic elements, they are more sensitive or difficult. What was it in Sarajevo? It was to harass the 50.000 troops in Sarajevo so that they stay on the Sarajevo front, and that they not be used by another commander on another front. This is a legitimate objective. How can you harass troops, military men, soldiers who, by the way, are in town, other than by opening fire on them? And if these men are not all on the front line, it would be much easier but they are scattered everywhere. What should a commander do? What should a military strategy or organisation do? They must take this legitimate objective into consideration and ensure that the actions undertaken be not actions that are, generally speaking, and this is very important, I insist on it, that generally speaking be actions causing too many civilian casualties because we know that that is a reality. But civilian casualties are inevitable in urban warfare. So as to the questions of the objective of harassing troops was legitimate or not, we say yes. Now, if you look at the figures, you know them, the Prosecution themselves produced those figures. Now, is that -- are these the proof of some unlawful action? We say no. But more than that we say that these figures were too low for this to be considered, not on the basis of one or two individual actions or -- but to believe that there was a campaign. 253 victims through sniping, as adduced by the Prosecution, P3137, yes, the 700 or -- 700 days of fighting and something around 932 casualties through shelling for the same period of time. Open your newspaper or yesterday's newspaper. Look at well known sites as provided by Amnesty International, who are neutral, and this is just by way of an example. Look at the recent conflict between Israel and the Lebanon. Over a month, from the 12th of July to the 14 of August, you already have more than a thousand civilian casualties. Take another very notorious side, very well known to specialists, the Iraqi body count. For the first three months of joint military operations, coalition-led operation in Iraq, you have from 7.000 to 10.000 civilian casualties in a supposedly clean war. So where is terror? Was there terror in Sarajevo? Such is the question. In order to ascertain whether there is terror, it's not enough to say any attack on civilians is terror. What you have to do is to clearly and as precisely as possible determine whether there were actions that were patently illegitimate and lawful which they were and what their results would have been. And what I say again about terror is that Sarajevo is the very example of the bad example, of the proper example. What do I mean? I mean this: When you look at Sarajevo, and I think that you come my way, Mr. Ierace, there were so many legitimate objectives in town that any attack, even a lawful one, a legitimate one, is going to cause terror, any legitimate attack in Sarajevo was bound to produce terror. In such a situation, how can you try to analyse what legitimate and lawful terror would be? After seeing a graph or a chart provided by Mr. Ierace where we see the comparison between the elements presented by the Prosecution and those eventually adduced by the Trial Chamber, I say this is impermissible. Why? Because at the end of the day, if you look at it, the most essential part is missing. We could look at it again, but I have it in mind. What is most essential in the Prosecution case? Which was lost here in this regard? It was the proof that terror was actually caused, not the lawful one but the unlawful one. The actual infliction of terror has totally disappeared from this chart.
