And this is quite strange. One dares to claim here that you no longer want to sustain this actually -- actual infliction of terror in your case. But we in our defence, we relied on your case as confirmed by the Tribunal in order to organise our own case, and because you had failed to prove -- and the actual infliction in Article 6 is important and it was not known, so we could have done away with this non-existent claim of terror. Let me go back to a point that is important with relation to Article 7, the problem of criminal responsibility due to command responsibility. I would like to draw your attention on some authorities as complied with by some countries, this is not an exhaustive list, but UK, Belgium, Canada, Spain, Italy, New Zealand, and the Netherlands. Do we with -- relate to the disproportionate character of an attack or to the lack of distinction, what should we do? Should we isolate one case or two, or do we look all of the attacks? What do you have in Sarajevo? We have a siege situation, encirclement, so there is also a situation of conflict, and we have a commander from September 1992 to September 1994. So what we have to do is not to look at the Markale marketplace in order to see whether there was a deliberate targeting. You have to look at all of the situation in order to see whether the command, in face -- faced with the situation had such a behaviour that norms and standards were not complied with. Statistics are very important in this respect because whatever your answer may be to the issue of terror, and you said it was impermissible to shell the city with mortar fire, we'll have to provide a clear answer to a simple question. Whilst there were so many cases of shell firing, and the mortar being an area zone, how can we have this result? And here I quote the Prosecution expert, who said that the overwhelming majority of victims in Sarajevo were males, old enough to fight, and men who were in the army. Or in the Territorial Defence. When you look at figures, when you look at Prosecution witnesses, expert witnesses, they claim that within this very close context of urban warfare, the results with regard to the overwhelming majority, I think it is vast majority as quoted in Exhibit P31, 3137, so that was that there was a vast majority of soldiers, therefore, a very small minority of civilians. Earlier on, a new document was quoted from Eckert [phoen] and Bekker, pertaining to the issue of customary international law or not. One thing has to be looked at in this respect. The said book was written in 2005. It's commentary in three volumes. But it fails to provide any answer to the question as to whether -- maybe apart from Yugoslav law, what this law was over 12 years ago. That is in the period 1992-94, at the material times. It is now said that this is the way it is now, but this is not a historic document, and you have to establish what prevailed then, and this is a major issue. All the more so since of course at the time General Galic could not imagine that we would, 12 years later, discuss this sort of issue because it was way beyond him anyway. So we'll have to see things in their historical context. You cannot take events and look at them today as if it came out of the blue. Page 72 mention is made of a strategy that lacks the art of discerning. I proved the contrary, so this is once again an error. And before I give the floor to Ms. Pilipovic, I'd like to mention a few things very briefly because witnesses were mentioned. But one thing is forgotten, one forgets to say what they said. Witness AD was mentioned by name very often. Namely that he had been given orders to shoot at the market outside of Sarajevo, and he had instructions to hit graveyards. But one thing was not told you, so one tries to hide that from you. Firstly, next to the marketplace, next door to it, there were barracks with a lot of police force. So we are very close to a possible target, and in the said graveyard there were trenches, defence trenches running along the graveyard, and the graveyards were used, the stones in the graveyard were used by the opponent as means of advances. So it's easy to say one hit or one didn't hit such and such elements. If you quote something, you have to quote extensively. I know I have to finish because I don't have that much time. One last reminder. With regard to this Trial Chamber judgement with regard to this case, you ever to look at the results of this alleged campaign but not based on just a couple of elements but on all of them. And the results are the figures, the truth, and they are very much in favour of the Defence case. I now give the floor to Ms. Pilipovic and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in response to the questions raised by my learned friend, Mr. Mark Ierace, I will first reply to the question pertaining to incident number 6. First of all, the panoramic photograph, the 360-degree photograph, cannot be used as evidence, and the Defence challenged all such photographs that the OTP used in their case during trial. Why did we do that? I will now go back to the issue of how necessary the on-site visit was, especially when it comes to this incident. Had the Trial Chamber gone to the site, they would have seen that there was a difference in the level of where the victim was and the bell-tower of the Orthodox church from where allegedly the victim was shot. When Defence went there, and we went there with our experts at least five times, we visited all of the sites scheduled in the indictment as well as the demarcation line between warring sides, which controlled certain parts of town, and on the basis of our experience there we could see that from the tower of the Orthodox church it was impossible to see the site where the victim was, nor was it possible to conclude that a person who was in that location could have had an unobstructed view of the location where the victim was. This is another very important fact which in view of the Defence had to be analysed and considered by the Trial Chamber. Also, they needed to establish whether there was an unobstructed view between the victim and the perpetrator. They also needed to establish whether there was something obstructing the view. They also needed to establish what was the exact distance from the source of fire to the location where the victim was. They also needed to question whether the distance was such as to enable whoever was shooting to see who the victim was and what was victim's capacity. So in view of the Defence, these were the objective standards that needed to be met, that needed to be established in relation to each individual incident in order to find out whether the person who pulled the trigger, and such persons were identified by the OTP in some cases and in some cases were not, so whether the person pulling the trigger intended indeed to kill or injury the victim. Another standard that the Trial Chamber failed to establish is the subjective standard, which is precisely the intention, the will of the person pulling the trigger. They needed to establish whether they wanted to kill or injure the victim or whether there was some unexplainable reason behind that. Once again, Defence wish to point out the fact that was neglected by my learned friend, which is just what a positive impact it would have had on the whole case had the Trial Chamber gone on an on-site visit. My learned friend spoke about the height of the Hrasno hill, explaining that from that position one could see the urban part of the town and that it was precisely from those positions that the members of the SRK fired upon the population of Sarajevo. This is the inference made by the OTP. The Defence made an on-site visit, and I told you that we went there at least five times, and we toured these positions. Had the Trial Chamber toured these positions, they would have seen that Ozrenska Street, which my learned friend mentioned as the street from which members of the SRK opened fire, goes from the western direction towards the Mojmilo hill, which was under the control of the ABiH army. To this day, there are still trenches that were put in place by the BH army. This is a fact supporting our position that this was held by the BH army. Had the Trial Chamber made an on-site visit, they would have seen that from that position one cannot see certain locations concerning which the Prosecution claims that the -- that it was from there that civilians in town were targeted. And they would be able to see that incidents 10, 15, 20 and 27 needed to be excluded as incidents for which the SRK members were responsible. Another issue that I should point is that my learned friend tried in his oral presentation today to tell the Appeals Chamber that unscheduled incidents to which my friend referred took place and that the Trial Chamber evaluated them within the scheduled incidents. I have to say that when it comes to the so-called unscheduled incidents, as my learned friend says, and for which they claim that they were part of the campaign, that such incidents were not discussed during trial, nor was it ever established or tried -- nobody even tried to establish how these incidents took place, nor did the OTP support this with any evidence. This is why the Defence claims that even if there were any incidents, then they could have been only a result of legitimate activity of the forces of the SRK and that under no circumstances should they be used to prove that there was a campaign against civilians. Thus I reply to my learned friend when it comes to incident number 6, we stand by our previous position that had the Trial Chamber visited the location, they would have established in relation to all other incidents that were discussed during trial that from the positions from which in view of the OTP the SRK forces opened fire, it was simply impossible to do that. This was not something that the SRK members were responsible for, these incidents. Now, in response to what my learned friend said about the hospital, I wish to say as follows: I wish to refer to the testimony of Witness D-51, who was a Defence witness. Your Honours, my learned friend is indicating that it may be time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: No. Why should we have a break?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you. When it comes to the position of the OTP and the presentation that my learned friend made about the Kosevo hospital, I wish to say as follows: In our presentation this morning, we said that the OTP witness stated that he received at least 25 protests and noticed that the hospital was used in order to fire upon the SRK forces. What is the Defence trying to say? Namely that the Defence -- that the members of army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were constantly warned not to use mortar fire from the hospital. Witness D-51, who was a Defence witness, and who continuously worked in the hospital at the time, also stated that in the hospital compound, there were three tanks and three combat vehicles. The witness stated that at all times when the BH army forces were active from the hospital compound the workers of the hospital had to vacate part of the hospital, had to evacuate the hospital because they were expecting a response from the SRK forces, because as the witness stated, after five or seven fired rounds, they would always receive a response in the same area, which would mean that the BH army forces were always, in advance, warned that there would be a response from those positions. So it is the view of the Defence that there cannot be a direct answer to the question put by the Appeals Chamber. I'm also hereby replying to my learned friend and reiterating that there was always due notice and warning that there should be no fire opened from the hospital compound. So this would be my reply when it comes to the issue of fire opened from the Kosevo hospital. I also mentioned D28, which was Defence Exhibit, a letter that we tendered into evidence during trial. Another issue that we wish to bring up in our response is the fact that in the final reports to which we referred this morning, certain facts were mentioned that we wished to repeat here before the Appeals Chamber once again. Namely, that back in 1993, the UN Commission of Experts established that the BH army forces concentrated their forces in town itself, that they conducted a very aggressive policy, that the SRK forces always uncovered the firing positions, I'm now referring to paragraph 37 of this report, and that they always opened fire only on legitimate and military targets. Another issue that I wish to mention is that it was necessary for each individual case to be evaluated separately so that they could exclude the possibility of randomness and error. And in this regard, we fully support the view of Judge Nieto-Navia, his position that was stated in his separate opinion. We also wish to reiterate that this general approach used by the OTP, namely when they say that civilians were regularly targeted when they went to fetch water, when they went to put out fires, when they sat in their homes, or attended funerals, once again, I emphasise that this is mere generalisation. The OTP, during trial, did not adduce a single piece of evidence that would support their claim that members of the SRK fired upon civilians when they went to fetch water, when they went to put out fires, when they picked lettuce, as mentioned when incident number 4. I also need to say that the OTP referred to the UNPROFOR members' evidence. In this regard, we need to say that all they stated was their opinion or their conviction. These witnesses, the ones referred to by the OTP, and this is something that we analysed in our appeals brief, these witnesses did not state in a single case that they were eye-witnesses to that incident, that they were present on the spot, that they saw the victims, or anything of the sort. We just heard what my learned friend said about the journalist who came here to testify, who came here and told us that he saw a woman who fell victim. This is yet another case of generalisation, and this Chamber said that such general claims cannot be used to support allegations of unlawful conduct. I also need to mention that the OTP, in all scheduled incidents, analysed before this Chamber, and we wish to reiterate our position that they are not reflective of the general situation in Sarajevo at the time. When it comes to all sniping scheduled incidents, we need to say that not in a single case did any member of SRK, let alone General Galic, receive notice that such an incident took place and who may have participated in it and who could have been the victim. I think that it is beyond dispute, I think that it was established beyond dispute by the Trial Chamber that demarcation lines between warring parties, that is to say the 1st Corps of the BH army, which at the time of its inception until the end of war had at least 30 brigades and that each brigade had at least 4.000 to 5.000 soldiers, nobody ever provided evidence that any member of the SRK received notice of these incidents, nor was it ever established that these incidents were caused by people who were in the positions controlled by the SRK forces. Let me give you a specific example. Incident number 2, the Prosecution adduced evidence by hearing witnesses, parents of a victim who allegedly died in the incident. No other evidence, apart from the evidence provided by these two witnesses, the parents, who are totally -- whose evidence was totally inconsistent, no other evidence was adduced, not even the showing of the map of this specific incident. That was identified by Mr. Karavelic, the 1st Corps commander, who marked every map regarding each separate incident to indicate where the demarcation lines were, so he was unable to mark the positions of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps on any of these maps, including the map that refers to incident 2. The Defence indeed referred to this incident in its appellate brief, and General Karavelic in fact only mentioned for this incident that this was no man's land. So it was impossible to determine the exact position of the SRK personnel and of the BH army personnel, so that we could say -- so that it could be said this is where they fired from. As far as the Jewish cemetery is concerned and the allegations that fire was opened from there, the Defence presented sufficient evidence, and in fact so did the Prosecution, regarding certain specific incidents. So, to be quite specific, from the positions at the Jewish cemetery, this is incident 24, it is incontestable that the positions both of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the BH army were in fact in the area of the Jewish cemetery, so we cannot rule out the possibility specifically talking about this incident 24 that in an area where combat was going on all the time, both in that part of the city and in fact throughout the city, that we cannot rule out the possibility there could -- that there could have been a stray bullet in an exchange of fire. Now, as regards incident number 5, the Defence and the Judge Nieto-Navia in fact claim that this was an incidental injury, in this case in fact the person died, the injured person died, but the majority of the Judges also do not rule out that there was a possibility that this was a ricochet. The majority took this into account but not to a sufficient extent. So in line -- in view of the standard set by the Chamber and the opinion of Judge Nieto-Navia, there is no evidence with regard to this incident and any other incident that was analysed and studied by the Defence to meet those standards, with regard to the sniping incidents so the Defence maintains that these incidents cannot be considered as part of the campaign, particularly not when it comes to the unscheduled incident that my learned colleague tried to make part of the incidents that were considered by the Chamber. The Defence will also say something about the views of the UN experts. The views -- the opinion that the Trial Chamber never in fact determined what was the military target in each military action, and we will also say something about the unscheduled incidents. We also would like to stress that because the part of the town controlled by the BH army forces, one could never rule out the collateral damage to civilian -- to civilians in those parts of the town, the Trial Chamber failed to take that into account. The Defence believes that it has responded in detail to all the issues raised by the Prosecution -- just a moment. I need to consult my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think we actually -- that this actually completes our presentation in response to the presentations by the Prosecution that we covered all the issues raised by them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Pilipovic. Is there any question from the Bench? If it's not the case, this concludes the consideration of the Defence appeal in this case. We'll now break and reconvene at 4.30 to consider the Prosecution appeal. The meeting is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So as scheduled, we will now resume to consider the appeal of the Prosecutor. I give the floor to the Prosecution for 20 minutes for their arguments.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And good afternoon to the Bench. This Chamber recently held in the ICTR decision of Gacumbitsi when substituting a sentence of life imprisonment in place of the Trial Chamber's 30-year one, and I quote from paragraph 205: "It is the Appeals Chamber's prerogative to substitute a new sentence when the one given by the Trial Chamber simply cannot be reconciled with the principles governing sentencing at the Tribunal." This is such a case calling for your exercise of that prerogative. A 20-year sentence is a manifestly inadequate one for a military commander in charge of a force of 18.000 men and a substantial weapon capacity, who used that force over a two-year period to order a campaign of deliberately indiscriminate and direct attacks against civilians in a city of 300.000 inhabitants, designed to cause terror to that population and which resulted in the deaths of hundreds of civilians, serious injury to several thousand more and the infliction of terror across that civilian population. The majority discernibly erred in its sentencing discretion when so deciding and we ask for the imposition of a life sentence to reflect General Galic's culpability. Our arguments are set out in full in our appeal brief, but today I will highlight the three most important reasons which show that the majority erred in imposing a 20-year sentence. Firstly, that the 20-year sentence fails to properly reflect the gravity of the crimes. Secondly, that it fails to properly reflect General Galic's role in ordering these crimes. And thirdly, that it fails to properly reflect the senior position which he abused to carry out these crimes. Turning first to the gravity of the criminal conduct, General Galic's crimes are among the worst to come before this Tribunal, and 20 years does not reflect their manifest gravity. In the Krstic case, this Appeals Chamber imposed a 35-year sentence on General Krstic for his role in aiding and abetting the massacre of several thousand men and boys in Srebrenica and deporting them from the region, all of which took place in the space of approximately one week. In the Stakic case, this Chamber imposed a sentence of 40 years on the mayor of a municipality, the Prijedor municipality, for his role in committing, through a joint criminal enterprise, a persecutory campaign of murder, imprisonment and deportation against civilians for a period of some five months. The mind generally finds it easy to comprehend the gravity of crimes of such magnitude when they occur in these relatively short time-frames. There is something about the instantaneousness of the crime which makes it so shocking. But why should a deliberate campaign conducted over a period of some years, two years, causing hundreds of thousands of people to live in fear for their lives every time they ventured out to conduct the most basic aspects of their lives and which caused the deaths of hundreds and serious injury to thousands of people be treated any more leniently? In our submission, it should not and the majority erred in doing so. First, Your Honours, the crime of terror itself must rank among the gravest of war crimes in this jurisdiction. Not only does it encapsulate the gravity which is associated with the unlawful attacks directed at civilians causing death or serious injuries, but it has the additional feature that these acts of violence are carried out with a particularly heinous purpose, to spread terror among the civilian population. Added to that, here, the terror was not merely aimed at but achieved, as is evident in the Trial Chamber's findings in paragraph 592 and 764. In fact, it was achieved so successfully that it really is difficult to properly capture the victimisation that took place in words, to say that the civilian population of Sarajevo, with its 300.000 inhabitants, was terrorised for two years seems hardly sufficient. Because what did this mean in practical terms for those inhabitants? Well, for many, it meant living in basements for most of the war. For those unfortunate enough to have to step out on to the streets, which was basically everyone at some point in time, because everyone must attend to the minimal necessities of life, such as getting water for themselves and their families, getting firewood for heating, tending to gardens to grow food, travelling to medical facilities to seek medical attention or attending the weddings or funerals of loved ones, it meant being exposed to the daily and deliberate sniper fire and the ever-frequent indiscriminate mortar attacks directed their way and the consequential state of fear that that engendered. Earlier today, in the presentation of my colleague, Ms. Jarvis, we heard a particularly compelling description given by Witness Henneberry who noticed frequent fire around supper time for no reason other than, and I quote from him, "Making people run building to building on their toes." To him, it was the application of psychological warfare on civilians, and it worked because they were, in his words and the words of many witnesses who gave evidence before the Trial Chamber, indeed terrorised and on edge. And for the thousands of people who were especially unlucky, it meant being subjected to serious injuries and indeed death. People who gathered at sporting events, at markets, even groups of children playing were frequently the target of mortars. People travelling through the city, using public transport, riding bicycles, trying to get across an intersection were targeted by sniper fire. And, as Mr. Ierace explained in his submissions, over time, the civilians did try and adapt to these miserable conditions and in some ways they got better at it. They learnt techniques such as putting up containers and others devices to try and protect themselves from the sniper fire, but the snipers even found ways around that; targeting victims when they have to leave their cover or could be seen through the gaps of the containers. Leaving to one side the gravity of what actually took place, the crimes that occurred in Sarajevo, the 20-year sentence also fails to properly reflect General Galic's role or participation in the crimes and nor the abuse of his very senior position which he engaged in to carry out that role. You'll recall that the majority found that he ordered these crimes. In our submission, it erred in not giving proper weight to the seriousness of this mode of his participation, this mode of his liability, when sentencing him to only 20 years' imprisonment. We are not speaking about ordering on one or two occasions. We are talking about Galic maintaining and continuing a campaign of this magnitude on a daily basis for the entirety of his two-year command. His mens rea was being refreshed on a weekly, if not daily basis by his receiving information as to the effects of this deliberate -- debilitating and destructive campaign. And in spite much evidence was heard from the UN and international witnesses about these protests, and in spite of regular, often daily protests from such representatives, Galic would instead cynically modulate the level of attack, oscillate it so as to adjust the outside perception of the campaign and thereby demonstrate even further his fine degree of command and control over the campaign's implementation. ICTY -- many cases before this Tribunal, such as Kordic, have acknowledged the seriousness of an ordering finding and its impact on sentencing, and last year in the Semanza case the Appeals Chamber increased that accused's sentence for ordering from 15 years to 25 years observing that, and I quote from the Semanza judgement: "A higher sentence is likely to be imposed on a principal perpetrator vis-a-vis an accomplice, in that case of genocide, and on one who orders rather than merely aids and abets exterminations." The final point I wish to address concerns General Galic's very senior position when he committed these crimes. Now, the Defence argues in its appeal against sentence, we didn't hear today from the Defence on its appeal against sentence, but one of its arguments there is that the majority erred in regarding as an aggravating factor the fact that he had a very senior position and repeatedly breached his public duty from this senior position, when it had already been encompassed or taken into account in the ordering conviction. The majority neither double counted this factor nor erred in treating his very senior position as an aggravating factor. In fact, as the Blaskic Appeals Chamber held in paragraph 91, where both Article 7(1) and 7(3) responsibility are alleged, and where the legal requirements pertaining to both are met, a Trial Chamber should enter a conviction on the basis of 7(1) only and consider the accused's superior position as an aggravating factor in sentencing. Indeed, in our submission, the majority erred in giving too little weight to his senior position as an aggravating factor. As corps commander, General Galic held one of the highest military positions in the army of the Republika Srpska. When he assumed command in September 1992, he inherited a pre-existing campaign to target civilians. And what did he do? As the commander of such a powerful military force of 18.000 men, did he protest or did he take steps to minimise the campaign? No, he did not. Did he ensure that his men acted within the minimal constraints on warfare mandated by international humanitarian law? No, he did not. To the contrary, he issued orders to his subordinates to continue that campaign, and in short, he used his very senior position to abuse the power entrusted to him, and this has not been sufficiently reflected in the sentence. To conclude, Your Honours, a 20-year sentence doesn't adequately reflect the nature and the scale of the crimes committed upon the civilians of Sarajevo, the protracted time-period in which they took place, Galic's daily renewal of his criminal involvement in the crimes, the extreme victimisation which resulted from this deliberate campaign, the very senior position he held and the seriousness arising both from the fact that he ordered this campaign and ordered it so as to spread terror. Finally, his subjected features are not such that they would mitigate a sentence of life imprisonment which can be, in the circumstances, the only condign one. Those complete my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Brady. Any questions? If there are none, I turn to the Defence for their submissions. You have 20 minutes for your submissions. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours. I have taken note of the submissions made by my colleague, and I will have make the following comments about them. First of all, I must repeat what I've already stated earlier on, that is that any procedure governed by international humanitarian law should never be based on the ruins, on the ashes of the rights of a human being and the right of an accused to defend himself as part of a fair trial. A number of things have been said just now. We've been told about the mens rea. We've been told that the rank and the functions of General Galic explain that he should be punished even more than he has been done, and we agree. We agree with the Prosecution that the Trial Chamber erred, but it erred not because it handed down a sentence of 20 years but because it handed down a sentence at all. Because what the Trial Chamber was to do was to acquit General Galic, and it was to acquit him based on this mens rea. Because instead of saying that what General Galic did in Sarajevo without knowing whether such and such attack, as Markale, was really a deliberate attack based on solid evidence, contrary to the evidence I quoted earlier on that show that he's not guilty, what had to be done was to consider what Galic did as part of this mens rea. We know that there aren't any written orders, there aren't any oral orders that would have been recorded, intercepted. Apparently he was not personally informed of any incidents. Henneberry, this witness was mentioned, but you forgot to mention that Henneberry was suffering from mental problems. He was not sure whether what he was saying was something he had really seen, experienced. You can check that whilst -- by reading the transcript of his testimony. We know that that witness had a notebook where he would take notes. And this Henneberry, this witness who was quoted so many times, he's the one who says that Galic was according -- acting according to a plan. But what does Henneberry say? Well, when you open his notebook, you find no trace of this supposed discussion with General Galic. And the witness Henneberry says, "Well, don't worry, I wrote to the United Nations," but then when you ask the Prosecution where are the complaints made to the United Nations, nothing comes up. There is nothing. So once again, I'd like to repeat it. If you want to use your witnesses, if you want to quote the witnesses, okay, but you have to do it in a comprehensive manner. If you are talking about witnesses who tried to talk and did talk to other witnesses before they are heard by the Chamber. Then these witnesses should not be considered, should not be taken into account. Now I'd like to move on to the following question. The fact that some things that General Galic did were not considered, things that cannot be part of the supposed plan alleged by the Prosecution. Let's take the example of the airport, firing at the airport. He's being told you're guilty because you fired at the airport. But what did General Galic do? When General Galic understood that the runways of the airport, that the Serbs had transferred to the United Nations for humanitarian purposes, when he realised that these runways were used by the BiH forces, what did he do? Did he fire on people? No. What he did was to get in touch with the United Nations officials and tell them, "But be careful, you are responsible now, you are responsible, you have to prevent that this airport that we transferred to you for humanitarian purposes is now used for other purposes. That's what he did. Can we really accept that such an action that -- which aim was to prevent civilian casualties is the proof of terror or of acts that are contrary to international humanitarian law? No. Did General Galic want to keep all this people imprisoned in Sarajevo in order to fire at them at random? No, not at all. General Galic, he's the man who was one of the first to design these famous blue roads in Sarajevo that were -- that would allow the population to leave without any risk. And we know that it's the opposing party that refused to accept that these roads should be organised in order to add a political element to the fight, to the war, and unfortunately they seemed to have won on that matter. Let me go back to another issue that I find very important as part of the examination of the mens rea, about the blind character, the random character of these shellings. You quoted Witness AD. I'm talking to the Prosecution. You quoted him, but you forgot to say that this witness, at the hearing, stated that when he refused to implement orders that he deemed unlawful, in other words he only obeyed orders that were lawful, then his commander did not punish these troops or refer the matter to the chain of command. What does that testimony prove? Two things. First of all, if nothing was reported, then General Galic did not know that these things had taken place. And secondly, when we are asked -- whether he was asked, this witness, why was the fact that you did disobey the order not reported to General Galic, the head of this battalion, this witness, says the following, he says, "Well, it's probably, it's probably because my commander, my superior officer, feared that he was going to be sanctioned, to be punished by General Galic." I think this is very, very clear. These words come from the mouth of Prosecution witnesses and not from Defence witnesses. Mr. President, I did not look at my watch when I started. How much time do I have left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to me, 13 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, 13 minutes. Thank you. Thank you very much. Yes. We've had a look at the humanitarian issues. We've had a look at the total exclusion zone. General Sibito [phoen], if I'm not mistaken, confirmed the matter at the time. This was implemented very quickly and within the time-frame set by General Galic. And another thing I'd like to mention was in the trial record, have we ever seen any evidence of a plan in writing or orally? No. There is no evidence to that effect. They decided to go in reverse order, maybe to reach someone else, but no plan was ever found. Yes, there is a document, that is, the minutes of a political meeting attended by General Galic. I don't have the exact reference here. But at the end of that meeting, and for the Prosecution apparently it's the only key document that proves that this plan existed, what does General Galic, at the end of this document -- at the time he was only a Lieutenant Colonel or a Colonel. General Galic stated the following. I've got the wording in English in front of me, but I'll quote it in Serbian, or from what I remember of the Serbian. He said, "We have to defend ourselves but 'bes rata,' without war." In other words, we have to defend ourselves without using the resources, the means of war. That's what General Galic said, and that's to be found in the exhibit that have been handed just now from the commander of the Partizan Brigade. Let me check that I've quoted this accurately. "Bes rama, bes rata," [phoen] in other words, defend without war. And this is Exhibit -- well, I can give you the electronic reference number, 00437694, 00437694. This is an exhibit that was produced on the 14th of May, 1992, but my copy is of too poor a quality for me to be able to read out, to make out the exhibit number. We can find it in the trial record. So these are the tangible, the actual, the practical elements, practical evidence that are supposed to prove that such a plan existed. In other words, Your Honours, nothing, we have nothing. All we have is something that proves that Galic wanted to defend himself without using -- without having recourse to war.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A quote in Latin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I have to come back to witnesses UN -- or to the UN witnesses to say the following: Yes, Galic was in command. And today, because the witnesses said that when there were complaints, Galic intervened for firing to stop. But now what is being told is that, no, not only he tried to control his troops, what is being said is that he tried to modulate pressure. This is a last resort theory that has been dreamt up by the Prosecution and that goes against the evidence. Let me give you the following transcript references: Page 11193 to 11196, Henneberry, this famous witness mentioned earlier on. Page 8572 to 8573, Hamill, who is quoted at paragraph 692 of the judgement. Transcript page 8460 and Exhibit DP35, transcript page 17731 and 177502, where we see that these witnesses all say that when meetings took place with General Galic, General Galic, what did he do? Well, he made sure that these meetings were translated into actions. There is also something that is very peculiar about the way the Tribunal has -- or the Trial Chamber has determined the mens rea of the accused. I'm thinking of what is at page 300 of the judgement, and I'm thinking of the considerations of the Trial Chamber with regard to Witness AD, who was clearly saying that his own superior did not complain because he thought that he was going to be punished by the higher chain of command or by the superior command of the corps. When the time comes for the Trial Chamber to analyse all this, it comes to the following conclusion, but we don't know why: The Trial Chamber comes to the conclusion that because the SRK corps, army corps, was perfectly organised, it can only be on the order of General Galic that this commander had opened fire. No other explanation is provided in the judgement. However, this is contrary to many other witness statements and testimony, including the testimony of a General - I have to quote from memory, but I'd like to point to his testimony - I'm talking about General Briquemont, who, when he came to testify here, stated, as a superior officer representing the United Nations, that he could not exclude - and I'm quoting from memory in English - could exclude that local chiefs, independent, had opened fire; in other words, without the knowledge and without the intervention of the corps commander. I have come to the end of my submissions. Let me just add the following. My colleague will now say a few words.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in response to the presentation of my learned friend, I would like first to point out an important fact. The Trial Chamber never established that there was a pre-existing campaign, which is something that the OTP claims that General Galic inherited, the pre-existing campaign, and no such statement exists in the trial judgement. So this is unsupported, what my learned friend said. What would I like to point out? I would like to point out that we stand by everything stated in our appeals brief and in our response. I would also like to mention mitigating factors, and I hope that this Appeals Chamber will take them into account, which is good character, lack of prior convictions of General Galic, and this is something established by the Blaskic trial, as well as General Galic's conduct in pre-trial detention where he spent six years. He came to the position of the corps commander from the rank of Colonel. He came overnight, if I may say so, to that position, due to the circumstances and the gravity of the situation in that area, where there was an urban warfare in place, where combat was extremely intense. General Galic overnight had to take over the role of the commander and thus found himself in the situation, and in the area where the conditions for command and control were more than difficult. Our military expert, Mr. Radinovic, spoke of these circumstances that made the role of General Galic extremely difficult. These are all the factors that we hope the Appeals Chamber will take into consideration. Regardless of the gravity of crimes, it is improper to render a sentence proposed by the Prosecution. Another mitigating factor that I would like to bring to your attention are the efforts of General Galic throughout the two years of his command to reconcile the interests of the two parties in that conflict. Throughout his position, throughout his mandate, he worked on disbanding paramilitary formations. The area of responsibility of General Galic was extremely complex and broad, and in that respect it was a limiting factor in terms of the efficiency of the command, chain of command. As a mitigating circumstance, I think that urban warfare needs to be taken into account as well. There was street-to-street combat, and warring sides acted against the Geneva Conventions and Geneva Protocols, paragraph 58. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. I give now the floor to the Prosecution for up to ten minutes to reply. You have the floor, Ms. Brady.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Our appeal against sentence proceeded on the basis of the factual findings which have been found by the majority. The response that we've just heard is essentially rechallenging the factual findings of the majority and a further attempt to argue what should have been argued in his main appeal. We've responded to all of these points in our response brief, so I won't go into that now. The other area that he traverses into is in relation to arguments in support of his sentence appeal, such as that he disbanded paramilitaries or supported the use of blue roads. And, again, Your Honours, I point you to our response in the response brief, ground 19, and there is no need to say anything further. I will hand over the floor to Mr. Ierace in just a moment, because I think there are some factual matters that have been raised which Mr. Ierace will address. But I wanted to just briefly speak to the one point he said about the fact that there was no mens rea, it wasn't found. And I point Your Honours to the conclusion of the majority in paragraph 745 of the judgement. The majority found that "the inference is compelling that failure to act for a period of approximately 23 months by a corps commander who has substantial knowledge of crimes committed against civilians by his subordinates and is reminded on a regular basis of his duty to act, upon that knowledge, speaks a deliberate intent to inflict acts of violence on the civilians." He said in passing that essentially no one was giving him notice of this or not sufficiently detailed notice of this. I draw Your Honours' attention to the dozens of UN witnesses who gave evidence to the contrary. Time wouldn't allow us to go through that right now, but if I could just point Your Honours at this stage to the evidence of Witness W, especially at transcript T-9565 to 9566 and T-9607 to 9608. The evidence was given in closed session so I'll be a bit cautious about how I refer to it and only refer to the details given in the trial judgement. But if he claims he had no notice of this, then this is a very difficult matter for him to explain. In effect, Witness W complained to Galic on an occasion when a water supply point had been shelled and caused many civilian casualties. Well, Galic's reply had so shocked Witness W, who was a senior UN representative, that he broke off all relations with Galic after that. And I quote from Witness W's testimony at T-9566, as cited in the judgement at paragraph 677, he said, "The explanations given to me by Colonel Galic, it seemed that it was his troops that had attacked the civilians, that his troops did act within the framework of his orders, that he considered it normal that his forces would attack civilians." He continued: "Therefore, I had full reason to describe this as a criminal act and I could not continue to have a dialogue with him in these circumstances." And he wasn't the only one. As I said, there were dozens of witnesses who gave evidence that they had made protests to Galic and very regularly. I'll turn now to Mr. Ierace who will respond to just a few points on the factual matters raised. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. Piletta-Zanin referred to the evidence of Witness AD, and suggested that my reference to his evidence had been somewhat incomplete. Specifically, Mr. Piletta-Zanin said that the evidence of that witness was that the orders to target civilian facilities, ambulances and the like, came from the brigade commander, but that he thought probably they did not emanate from the accused, from the appellant. That, in fact, was speculation. The witness's evidence was that he didn't know where the orders came from, going up the ranks beyond the office of the brigade commander, and so anything he said beyond that was speculation. Mr. Piletta-Zanin also referred to what one might broadly call the peaceful humanitarian acts of the appellant in support of his contention that he's not guilty of these charges. He referred to the setting up of blue routes and the desire for peace. The setting up of the blue routes occurred in the atmosphere post the Markale market incident. The international outrage at that carnage was such that the SRK came under considerable pressure to agree to UN-managed routes of humanitarian aid into the city; and, secondly, the setting up of a total exclusion zone of heavy weaponry to some distance, some 20 kilometres from the city. There was nothing voluntary in that sense about what the appellant did. He was responding to the pressure from the international community. In a similar vein, whilst he agreed from time to time to anti-sniping agreements, they weren't worth the paper they were written on, as is demonstrated by scheduled sniping incident number 27, a 13-year-old boy shot whilst window shopping with his family, five or six children playing nearby. Why were they outside on that occasion? Because there was an anti-sniping cease-fire which meant nothing. That was an incident found proved by the Trial Chamber. In relation to the handing over of the airport by the SRK, that happened pre the indictment period and again ultimately as a result of a UN Security Council resolution, 762, which charged UNPROFOR with protecting the airport. And in those circumstances, following that resolution, the SRK handed over the airport. Mrs. Pilipovic, just before the break, referred again to sniping incident 6 and said that there was no evidence of a line of sight from the bell tower to where the victim was shot. The 360-degree photograph demonstrates otherwise when looked at in conjunction with the marked photographs and further photographs that were tendered in relation to that incident. Mr. Piletta-Zanin has again referred, as I understand it, to the incidents of civilian casualties as some sort of evidence of the innocence of the appellant, and it is not such evidence. It reflects, as the majority found, various anti-sniping and anti-shelling measures taken by the populace, and also that there was not a constant barrage with the primary aim of killing as many civilians as possible. That was never the Prosecution case. The Prosecution case was that the intention of the appellant was to inflict terror. He did not need in order to achieve that aim to attempt to kill every civilian in the city, and indeed it would have been very difficult for him to act with that objective when he was under the watchful eye of the international community represented as it was by the UN military observers. He had to be far more careful than that and it was only the occasional mortar shell lobbed into the city, any time, anywhere, that could maintain that fear entertained by every Sarajevan civilian that they or their loved ones could be killed any time anywhere. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. This concludes --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to make any comments, Mr. President, but there was a problem in the translation. Yes, thank you. I'm not going to make any comments because I'm not entitled to do so, but I would like to stress that there was a major translation problem, when what Ms. Pilipovic said at line 1131, it was not that both parties to the conflict committed acts contrary to the Geneva Conventions, but what she said was that the ABiH army behaved contrary or in contravention to Article 58 of Protocol 1. That's what Ms. Pilipovic wanted to say, and there was a problem in the translation with respect to that comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. We take note of that for the record. As I was saying, this concludes both appeals, the Defence appeal and the Prosecution appeal. Before closing the hearing, Mr. Galic, if he so wishes, may address personally the Bench for a maximum of 15 minutes. So I turn to Mr. Galic. Do you want to address the Bench?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have full trust in justice, and I believe in what my Defence presented here in court, and I have full trust in the authorities that will make the final judgement in this matter. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Galic. Well, that concludes our hearing today. We will now adjourn and the judgement will be rendered in due course. The meeting is adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.17 p.m.
